Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/stocks-are-driving-consumption-like-never-before--and-that-exposes-a-big-risk-100000963.html
The stock market isn't the economy in the way that Nvidia's share price won't help your nephew find a job, or save for a down payment, or afford double meat and guac at Chipotle.
There's a level of abstraction and distance from day-to-day, working-class life that can make stock watching seem exotic. But the enormous gains of equity holdings in recent years have changed the makeup and definition of wealth in the US, with even bigger implications.
In a way that has only become true in our moment, the stock market actually is getting closer to defining the economy and consumption.
That's one of the key arguments in a note by Doug Peta, chief US investment strategist at BCA Research, published on Monday.
"The stock market isn't the economy, but it's influencing it like never before," he wrote. Peta observed that household net worth was over eight times disposable income at midyear, marking an all-time high for that measure. For decades, Wall Street has delivered outsized, compounding returns, making equities and mutual funds an ever-greater portion of household wealth.
The value of households' equity stake is nearly three times their annual after-tax income, Peta found. That means the S&P 500 gaining 10% in a year boosts a household's capacity to spend equivalent to receiving a 28% raise.
As a result, Peta wrote, stock market moves can swing consumption and overall economic activity. Combined with sharp home price appreciation, surging portfolios have augmented consumers' firepower far more than in any previous cycle, he said.
This helps explain the years-long narrative of the resilient American consumer. The people who spent their way through COVID, the aftermath, and sustained periods of high inflation. Stocks making up a higher share of a household's net worth has meant consumption is more sensitive to equity market moves. In good times, stock upswings can override other factors weighing down the economy.
"Greater sensitivity has been a boon for activity in the current cycle, as increasing equity wealth has allowed households to spend more of their paychecks than they otherwise may have," Peta wrote.
But that sensitivity is two-sided.
If the way the Wall Street winds are blowing has a greater say on the American consumer — because stock holdings increasingly define American wealth — that means the next bear market will have amplified influence.
Because instead of people feeling rich and spending through it, they will feel vulnerable and pull back.
In that very real sense, the stock market and the economy would sink together.

item.title: Last week saw the largest tech sell skew in more than 5 years, Jefferies says
item.author: Jake Conley
item.description:
Last week saw the largest tech sell skew in more than 5 years, Jefferies says
2026-10-20
Por Jake Conley
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/last-week-saw-the-largest-tech-sell-skew-in-more-than-5-years-jefferies-says-173834306.html
Jefferies' equity trading desk saw its most heavily selling-tilted tech trading week in more than five years, analysts said over the weekend, putting a finer point on the CoreWeave-led tech sell-off that dominated markets last week.
"Simply put, there's a tremendous amount of angst in the market right now, and from our conversations and flows, there's been a very consistent and violent de-gross occurring over the last several sessions," Jeffrey Favuzza, TMT equity strategist at Jefferies, wrote to clients.
By market close on Friday, the week's skew in tech equities had reached $7.5 billion in net selling activity — a significant jump over the $5.5 billion skew ahead of the opening bell on Friday and a testament to heavy selling into the weekend.
The jump in outflow activity was enough to push the week's skew past that of the "DeepSeek moment" week in January 2025, when the Chinese AI lab released its open-weight DeepSeek model and set off a flurry of concerns that US labs would see their revenues fall as enterprises turned to cheaper foreign options, the analysts said.
Selling activity through Jefferies' equity trading desk was most concentrated last week in semiconductors, memory, hardware, and communications equipment subsectors, Favuzza noted, while only horizontal software and IT/info services subsectors saw a notable buy skew on the week.
That split matched activity in the wider market, where the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell by roughly 3% while the Philadelphia Semiconductor index (^SOX) lost 10%.
Much of the problem, Favuzza noted, lies with an increasingly sketchy financing picture. Part and parcel of the AI boom is the explosion in capex across the sector, with capex by hyperscalers alone expected to exceed $800 billion in 2026 and cross $1 trillion next year.
That spending has collided with a range of factors — the war in Iran, growing US debt, trade turmoil — that have pushed the international bond complex into a deep sell-off, sending yields on government debt from the US and other nations to multi-decade highs "at the same time that the hyperscalers have flooded the market with paper this year."
Last week's sell-off was largely catalyzed by spiking credit risk and worries about the worthiness of debt issuance at CoreWeave (CRWV), a so-called neocloud that's heavily backed by Nvidia (NVDA).
"While the underlying demand for the Neos hasn't downticked," Favuzza wrote to clients, "the confidence in some of their access to cheaper capital has."
The tech trade has also lost some of the momentum-driven wind in its sails, Favuzza said, arguing that "we never recovered, both from a price and conviction standpoint, from the Momentum meltdown of the summer." Not only was last week the worst in more than five years by sell skew, but it was also the second-worst week for the tech momentum pair (buying winning tech stocks while selling losers) in more than 20 years, beaten out only by a COVID-19 sell-off.

item.title: Goldman Sachs is still betting on a nice year-end rally for the S&P 500
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Goldman Sachs is still betting on a nice year-end rally for the S&P 500
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/goldman-sachs-is-still-betting-on-a-nice-year-end-rally-for-the-sp-500-134755098.html
Momentum tech stocks tied to the AI boom may be triggering market tremors, but Goldman Sachs still thinks the year will end just fine for investors.
In a new note, Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider maintained his 8,000 year-end S&P 500 (^GSPC) price target. His target assumes about 5% upside from the current level of 7,659.
If Snider was concerned about an AI bubble bursting — as investors on X are chatting about seemingly around the clock — he isn't showing it in his 2027 S&P 500 target either. He sees the S&P 500 wrapping up next year at 8,700.
"Positive but decelerating growth has historically been associated with positive but moderating S&P 500 returns. Equity returns in these environments have historically been driven by earnings growth rather than by valuation expansion," Snider said.
Snider is modeling for 36% earnings growth for the S&P 500 this year, cooling to an 11% increase in 2027.
Snider's defense of a solidly bullish outlook comes as the very driver of markets this year — tech stocks playing a key role in the AI boom — fall under increased scrutiny by investors.
The returning concern: Revenue may not match the billions of dollars companies are investing in AI. How that unfolds for companies using massive amounts of debt to fund their AI investments is a top worry right now.
AI chip darling Nvidia (NVDA) shed more than $350 billion in market value last week. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOXX) plunged more than 11%.
Neocloud CoreWeave (CRWV) shed 25% on the week amid rising borrowing costs.
"This [move in CRWV] is more sentiment-driven. This is not about fundamentals," BofA analyst Tal Liani said on Sozzi Unleashed. "This is not about them not being able to pay for the debt, et cetera. This is more sentiment-driven, and the sentiment needs to change. And what's going to happen is, as always, there's going to be a period of concern. And then the fundamentals will kick in, meaning revenues, revenue growth."

item.title: Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Elon Musk says he's giving SpaceX stock to every kid in America
2026-10-20
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/elon-musk-says-hes-giving-spacex-stock-to-every-kid-in-america-131435467.html
Kids will soon have a financial interest in the future of space.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX (SPCX) shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said in an X post on Monday.
Musk didn't specify an age range for the proposed gift, but a Bloomberg report indicated he could use Trump Accounts as the vehicle for his stock donations.
SpaceX stock rose 1% in morning trading on Monday.
There are currently about 73 million children under 18 living in the US, according to the latest Census Bureau data. That number goes down to about 18.5 million for newborns up to 4 years old.
SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell has already pledged a personal donation of more than $320 million in SpaceX stock to fund Trump Accounts for more than 2 million children.

item.title: Palantir, Datadog and chip stocks bounce back as Amazon lifts Wall Street
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Palantir, Datadog and chip stocks bounce back as Amazon lifts Wall Street
2026-10-20
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/palantir-datadog-and-chip-stocks-bounce-back-as-amazon-lifts-wall-street-204043191.html
Tech stocks got off the mat Monday. Most of Wall Street stayed pinned down.
Palantir (PLTR) and Datadog (DDOG) jumped over 4% each, joined by Snowflake (SNOW) and a broad recovery in chip stocks after last week's beating.
Western Digital (WDC) and Sandisk (SNDK) led the storage rally, while Micron (MU), Intel (INTC), and Nvidia (NVDA) also gained. More than 9 in 10 semiconductor names and roughly 4 in 5 software stocks advanced in Yahoo Finance's watchlists.
Buyers had fresh encouragement. Bernstein upgraded Datadog, citing stronger AI-related demand. Palantir announced a government-cloud partnership, although its rebound reached a potential selling zone around $195–$200. Getting through that area would put its recent record high back in play and lend support to the broader recovery after last week's failed breakouts.
Amazon (AMZN) supplied some heavyweight help. Shares climbed 5%, recovering last week's losses after Morgan Stanley named the company a top pick. Tesla (TSLA) also rallied.
Together, those gains helped the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rise 1.1%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) add 0.4%.
But buyers weren't handing out second chances to everyone.
"We can't just go and buy all the AI companies because they all dipped," Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, told Yahoo Finance.
CoreWeave (CRWV) provided a case in point. Its early rally after a Goldman Sachs upgrade to Buy disappeared. Shares finished slightly lower at $61.12, just above July's closing low of $60.82.
The trouble wasn't limited to CoreWeave. Nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks fell, and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) lost ground. The broader index rose, but most of its stocks fell.
Tuesday's test is whether more stocks join the rebound and CoreWeave can pull away from its July low.

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/palantir-datadog-and-chip-stocks-bounce-back-as-amazon-lifts-wall-street-204043191.html

Tech stocks got off the mat Monday. Most of Wall Street stayed pinned down.

Palantir (PLTR) and Datadog (DDOG) jumped over 4% each, joined by Snowflake (SNOW) and a broad recovery in chip stocks after last week's beating.

Western Digital (WDC) and Sandisk (SNDK) led the storage rally, while Micron (MU), Intel (INTC), and Nvidia (NVDA) also gained. More than 9 in 10 semiconductor names and roughly 4 in 5 software stocks advanced in Yahoo Finance's watchlists.

Buyers had fresh encouragement. Bernstein upgraded Datadog, citing stronger AI-related demand. Palantir announced a government-cloud partnership, although its rebound reached a potential selling zone around $195–$200. Getting through that area would put its recent record high back in play and lend support to the broader recovery after last week's failed breakouts.

Amazon (AMZN) supplied some heavyweight help. Shares climbed 5%, recovering last week's losses after Morgan Stanley named the company a top pick. Tesla (TSLA) also rallied.

Together, those gains helped the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rise 1.1%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) add 0.4%.

But buyers weren't handing out second chances to everyone.

"We can't just go and buy all the AI companies because they all dipped," Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, told Yahoo Finance.

CoreWeave (CRWV) provided a case in point. Its early rally after a Goldman Sachs upgrade to Buy disappeared. Shares finished slightly lower at $61.12, just above July's closing low of $60.82.

The trouble wasn't limited to CoreWeave. Nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks fell, and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) lost ground. The broader index rose, but most of its stocks fell.

Tuesday's test is whether more stocks join the rebound and CoreWeave can pull away from its July low.

item.title: John Ternus Is Engineering a New Era for Apple: The Best Inventions of 2026
item.author: Andrew R Chow; Cupertino; Calif
item.description:
John Ternus Is Engineering a New Era for Apple: The Best Inventions of 2026
2026-10-20
Por Andrew R Chow; Cupertino; Calif
https://time.com/collection/best-inventions/2026/apple-iphone-duo/
Just below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking.
On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. Winning over the 21-year-old isn’t exactly the toughest assignment Ternus has faced in his 25-year Apple career: Speed barks when he sees the phone and then gleefully springs into a backflip.
Ternus, who took over as CEO on Sept. 1, was chosen to run Apple because he has ably applied his engineering and design expertise to shape products that redefined entire categories of technology, from the Mac to iPad to AirPods and the iPhone. But becoming the face and front man for the second biggest company in the world by market cap is another proposition entirely. Ternus’ hard technical skills may not translate easily to a position that involves toggling from Hollywood to stockholders, to politicians shaping policy, to rival CEOs in the constellation of tech companies whose power challenges nation-states.
His predecessor, Tim Cook, gained stature on the world stage as a power broker deftly navigating global politics, markets, and supply chains. Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, was a rock-star visionary who sold the world on the deeply personal and even spiritual nature of tech creations. Ternus is different from both: a private, detail-oriented engineer, little known outside the company until he became a senior hardware executive in 2021.
Rather than try to replicate his forerunners’ styles of success, Ternus has so far played to his own strengths—which are also those of Apple, a company that first and foremost builds beautiful products that spark productivity, creativity, and joy. Ternus’ interaction with IShowSpeed is clearly designed to capture this (and, of course, to goose preorder numbers among the influencer’s young and massive audience). To some critics, however, the scene might read as a legacy company aura-farming to sell expensive gizmos instead of building the actual technological future, which is artificial intelligence.
Virtually every one of Apple’s fellow Goliaths—Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, and now Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years. At the end of September, Apple was conspicuously absent when President Donald Trump hosted a luncheon for AI power players like SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s Sundar Pichai, who lobbied him on their visions for America’s tech future.
But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it. And besides, Ternus argues, even if other companies succeed in their mission of building super-intelligence, users will still want to talk to it on Apple devices.
“People want physical things,” he says a week later at the company’s flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York City, wearing an amiable but guarded smile. He spent the morning greeting superfans who
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Netflix faces questions on user engagement ahead of third-quarter report
item.author: Reuters
item.description:
Netflix faces questions on user engagement ahead of third-quarter report
2026-10-20
Por Reuters
https://finance.yahoo.com/media-advertising/articles/netflix-faces-questions-user-engagement-101735340.html
Oct 19 (Reuters) - Netflix investors are expecting details on how the streaming giant plans to sustain growth when it reports third-quarter results on Tuesday, as competition intensifies and user engagement shows signs of fatigue.
Ted Sarandos, the co-CEO of Netflix, recently admitted the company "is not growing as fast as I want us to", and suggested live programming could be an opportunity to accelerate growth.
Here are more details:
• Netflix is expected to post its slowest third-quarter revenue growth in three years, with sales forecast to increase 11.8% to $12.87 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
• It cut about 6% of its workforce in a move that analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer said reflected the streaming industry's shift to profitability.
• Netflix also saw a change in its content leadership, with longtime head of content Bela Bajaria leaving the company and former Disney executive Peter Rice taking over.
• Its US user churn rose 16.6% year-over-year in the third quarter, roughly double the pace of the prior three quarters, while downloads in the US and Canada fell 20%, according to market research firm Apptopia.
• Jefferies estimates average monthly viewing time per Netflix member fell to 49 hours in the first half of this year from 66 hours in the first half of 2023.
• The 2026 FIFA World Cup and a weaker content slate than last year weighed on Netflix's engagement, analysts said.
• The company recently acquired broadcast rights to air the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra.
• Netflix is betting on advertising to diversify revenue, with Jefferies forecasting ad revenue to reach $7.5 billion in 2029.
(Reporting by Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru; Editing by Edmund Lee and Devika Syamnath)

item.title: Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad
2026-10-19
Por Texto propio
# Why Is Tech Billionaire Marc Andreessen So Mad?
October 15, 2026
The prominent investor has said the Biden administration pushed him to the political right, but sources say his grievances don't always match reality.
By Austin Carr
Marc Andreessen sounded angry. It was May 22, 2024, and he was venting to a table full of President Joe Biden's officials in the West Wing office of Jeff Zients, then the White House chief of staff. The famed venture capitalist was in town with his longtime investing partner, Ben Horowitz, to discuss US tech policy, and the private lunch soon turned heated. Andreessen expressed his frustration about a slew of Biden administration initiatives and regulations, especially ones he believed were crippling the artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency industries. Near the end of the lunch, he also launched into a tirade against a Democratic proposal to hike taxes on the wealthiest 0.01% of American households. "The billionaire tax seemed to offend him more than anything we'd done on AI or even crypto," says Bruce Reed, one of the handful of White House advisers who had joined the meeting.
Forgotten, at least, until Donald Trump won the election months later and Andreessen revealed in the aftermath the crazy reason why he had unexpectedly plowed millions of dollars into the Make America Great Again movement during the campaign. Andreessen, who voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and said back then that Trump's immigration regime "makes me sick to my stomach," explained on a podcast that he was compelled by "absolutely horrifying" discussions he once had with Biden officials. In his retelling, they divulged a top-secret plan for the federal government to take control of the AI industry and outlaw all startups and open-source software. "You guys think you can just start companies and write code and release code on the internet—those days are over," he remembered them warning in the meeting.
Andreessen was so aghast that he felt it was in the best interest of his firm, Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as a16z, to publicly endorse Trump. "They're going to kill us," Andreessen recalled thinking on Ross Douthat's podcast in January 2025. "We walked out and stood in the parking lot of the West Wing and took one look at each other, and we're like, 'Yeah, we're for Trump.'" (Horowitz later hedged his support when Kamala Harris replaced Biden in the race, and he made a significant personal donation.)
The incident became Silicon Valley lore, but at first the Biden-Harris camp couldn't even figure out what meeting Andreessen was referring to, according to four people familiar with the situation. When they finally realized he was talking about the lunch in Zients' office, those who attended were baffled: Andreessen is prone to hyperbole, but this neared complete fiction. "It is simply false that the Biden administration told Andreessen and Horowitz that the government would ban all AI startups," says Ben Buchanan, then a special adviser to the president on AI, who attended the May 22 meeting. It also made little sense why Andreessen hadn't asked about this astonishingly draconian plan at a meeting on May 24 with national security advisers including Anne Neuberger. (Neuberger, whom a16z has since hired, declined to comment.) As another top Biden official familiar with their visits told colleagues of Andreessen's version of events: "Total bulls---."
A representative for Andreessen, Horowitz and a16z's government affairs chief, Collin McCune, who also attended the contentious meeting in DC, has said the firm stands by their recollections. (Horowitz and McCune didn't respond to requests for comment for this article.) Whatever actually occurred at that lunch matters less than what's happened since: a16z, known for Andreessen once proclaiming that "software is eating the world," is now eating the political world. The dominant VC firm, wh
[Transcripcion recortada]

It also made little sense why Andreessen hadn't asked about this astonishingly draconian plan at a meeting on May 24 with national security advisers including Anne Neuberger. (Neuberger, whom a16z has since hired, declined to comment.) As another top Biden official familiar with their visits told colleagues of Andreessen's version of events: "Total bulls---."
A representative for Andreessen, Horowitz and a16z's government affairs chief, Collin McCune, who also attended the contentious meeting in DC, has said the firm stands by their recollections. (Horowitz and McCune didn't respond to requests for comment for this article.) item.author: Thomas Kent
item.description:
Peter Schiff warns a ‘perfect storm of financial destruction’ worse than 2008 is brewing. Build wealth beyond your home
2026-10-19
Por Thomas Kent
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/peter-schiff-warns-perfect-storm-110500854.html
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.
The low mortgage rate you locked in years ago might be one of your best financial decisions. Peter Schiff argued it could also be part of a "perfect storm of financial destruction that is about to hit."
"Mortgage lenders will lose far more during the developing mortgage crisis than they did during all of the GFC," Schiff warned in an Oct. 15 post on X (1), referring to the global financial crisis.
A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Priority Gold's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free
He claimed, "Even without a single default, on paper mortgage lenders have already lost over four times more than they lost during the GFC."
He blamed the Federal Reserve's prolonged low interest rates and government-backed mortgages that let borrowers lock in cheap financing for decades.
"That sowed the seeds," he wrote.
An alarming forecast, especially if your home represents much of your wealth or you're counting on your investments to carry you through retirement.
But before you start picturing another foreclosure crisis, there's an important distinction: A mortgage losing value to an investor doesn't automatically mean your house has lost value, your payment is going up, or your lender is about to fail.
And keep in mind, if your loan or its servicing changes hands, the new company can't just rewrite your agreement (2).
Why Schiff sees trouble in low-rate mortgages
"There is currently about $8.3 trillion in outstanding fixed-rate mortgages with an average rate of 4.6% and 25 years left to maturity," Schiff wrote. "Given that current rates are 7.5%, the mark-to-market losses on those mortgages are already about $2 trillion. When rates rise to 8.5%, the loss will rise to $3 trillion!"
For comparison, Schiff put realized losses on defaulted mortgages during 2007–2010 at about $450 billion.
Keep in mind these are Schiff's estimates, and his 8.5% scenario isn't today's reality. The latest Freddie Mac survey (3), released Oct. 15, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.40%, up from 6.27% a year earlier.
Here's the basic pricing problem: If a new mortgage pays a substantially higher rate, an investor generally won't pay full price for an otherwise comparable older loan paying much less. The older loan then needs a discount to compete.
That decline in market value is the paper loss Schiff is describing. The homeowner could still be making every payment on time.
Schiff puts two different types of losses side by side — money lost when borrowers default, and declines in what performing loans could fetch in a sale.
A mortgage can lose resale value even while homeowners keep making payments. That can hurt whoever owns the loan, but it isn't the same as a borrower defaulting.
Who owns the loan matters. Mortgages are often sold and packaged into securities (4) whose investors receive payments from pools of borrowers. So, the company that originated your mortgage isn't necessarily the one carrying its investment risk going forward.
You don't have to accept Schiff's prediction to examine your own exposure. If your home accounts for much of your wealth, how much have you built outside it?
Consider gold alongside your other assets
If much of your wealth is tied up in property, building investments outside housing can give you exposure to different sources of returns.
A gold IRA is one option for adding physical precious metals to your retirement portfolio. Gold is often used as a potential hedge against inflation and economic uncert

item.title: Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
item.author: Jason Ma
item.description:
Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
2026-10-19
Por Jason Ma
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/official-data-show-china-dumping-175844985.html
China was once the top holder of U.S. Treasuries but has been shedding its massive stockpile for years, fueling fears of de-dollarization, but official data may not fully capture Beijing's actual portfolio.
The decline began in earnest around 2021, but as recently as April 2022, China still held $1 trillion in Treasury securities. U.S. data on Friday show that's been whittled down to just $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier.
But the data is collected primarily from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, according to the Treasury Department, which adds that U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to the actual owners.
As a result, China watchers have long been skeptical of a wholesale dumping of U.S. assets, pointing to suspicious jumps in Treasury holdings elsewhere that coincide with the steep Chinese drop.
Canada's holdings soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion in the same month five years ago. Similarly, Belgium's stockpile shot up to $490.5 billion from $228 billion over the same span. After including other bonds backed by federal housing agencies, the numbers are even more staggering.
To be sure, China has been challenging the U.S. for supremacy in global finance, seeking to unseat the dollar as the world's top currency.
U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine further encouraged the People's Bank of China and other central banks around the world to diversify away from dollar reserves and toward alternative assets like gold.
President Donald Trump's trade war, which has been particularly focused on China, gave Beijing more reasons to ditch Treasuries and decouple from the U.S.
But at the same time, China has relied more heavily on export-led growth in recent years as domestic demand remains stagnant amid the festering property crash and debt hangover.
So despite the friction with the U.S. and other trade partners, China posted a $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025—the largest in recorded history—growing three times faster than global goods trade.
This year looks to break that record. For the first nine months of 2026, China's trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year's milestone.
Such massive surpluses must be recycled back somewhere, perhaps leading China to shift its Treasury debt to non-U.S. custodian banks in other countries—and not show up as "China" in official U.S. data.
"The evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong — note the sudden jump in Canada's holdings and the big impact of the detailed June survey at some early points," Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Treasury official, posted on X on Wednesday while highlighting a Bloomberg story on the subject.

item.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
item.author: Alice Cunningham
item.description:
Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
2026-10-19
Por Alice Cunningham
https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c9m26kl5y7epo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D
Microsoft pulls out of UK's largest AI data centre
A tech company has said it still plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre despite Microsoft pulling out of the project.
Nscale announced last year it had pledged £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex.
However, the BBC understands that Microsoft, which said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has terminated its involvement.
A spokesperson for Nscale said it was exploring alternative power sources and its relationship with Microsoft remained strong for their other projects together overseas. Microsoft declined to comment.
"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," Nscale said.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term."
The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of the year.
But as first reported by the Telegraph on Sunday, Nscale has been told this will not happen until the 2030s.
"This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," Nscale told the BBC.
Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States.
The Loughton site is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it eventually opens.
Only last month, Microsoft announced that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it was investing in the UK would be used to fund the Loughton supercomputer.

item.title: The next AI race will be won at the credit desk
item.author: Mehran Gul
item.description:
The next AI race will be won at the credit desk
2026-10-19
Por Mehran Gul
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/next-ai-race-won-credit-210000006.html
In August, Nvidia pulled together six of the biggest names in finance—Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR—to set up financing platforms that could mobilize over $500 billion for companies building AI infrastructure. It was the latest move by a company that has gone from making chips to orchestrating the wider playing field in AI—and a sign that growth for the world's most valuable company depends as much on the next big engineering challenge as on whether customers can keep affording its products.
It also points to the wider direction of travel in AI. Even as the world obsesses about model releases, chip capabilities, and data center capacity, the variable that increasingly determines who gets to compete is simply money. The next phase of the AI race between companies and countries will depend in large part on who can pay for it; the action is shifting from frontier labs to credit desks. Whoever can raise capital cheaply and at scale will set the pace, and that race still favors the United States, whose capital markets are deeper than anyone else's. For China and Europe, the road to closing the technological gap runs through the financial one.
Technological revolutions tend to be remembered for their technologies: steam engines, railways, the internet. Just as important is the financial machinery that made them possible: the joint-stock company dispersed the risk of trading voyages; early bond and equity markets financed railroads before they could produce a return; venture capital supplied high-risk money to companies too new to raise it from traditional investors.
AI is reaching its own version of this moment. For half a century, technology was asset-light: software could be written once and distributed to billions at negligible marginal cost. AI is turning technology into a heavy industry. The latest systems require factories, advanced chips, substations, and enormous supplies of electricity. Even the world's richest companies are finding it hard to fund all of this from their income.
The five largest American hyperscalers alone are on track to spend $730 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. A shrinking proportion is coming from their own balance sheets; they are expected to finance up to a third of it with debt.
If the most profitable companies in history have to borrow to stay in the race, what hope is there for everyone else?
Nvidia's deal is one answer. Project finance has long funded infrastructure with high up-front costs, paid down by steady returns over many years: power plants, toll roads, airports. What's new is the attempt to turn compute into an asset class that pension funds and insurers are comfortable owning, the way they already own infrastructure.
The arrangement carries risks. The parallel with infrastructure is imperfect: Energy facilities are built to last decades, usually in response to foreseeable demand, and generate predictable returns. In contrast, graphics processing units (GPUs) are short-lived assets; AI demand is unpredictable; and it is too early to project returns.
Still, if the upsides from AI are speculative, so are the downsides—and if the model works, it could reshape the AI market much as venture capital changed the risk calculus for starting a business.
Nvidia's announcement came with familiar worries about circular financing, in which the chipmaker's money comes back to it as chip orders. But this arrangement is the opposite. Nvidia will not, for the most part, be lending its own money—nor will its six partners. The capital comes from third parties: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, household savings. Rather than a closed loop, the buildout is being wired into the wider financial system: the deal does not artificially boost demand but restructures the cost of supply f

AI is turning technology into a heavy industry. The latest systems require factories, advanced chips, substations, and enormous supplies of electricity. Even the world's richest companies are finding it hard to fund all of this from their income.

The five largest American hyperscalers alone are on track to spend $730 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. A shrinking proportion is coming from their own balance sheets; they are expected to finance up to a third of it with debt.

If the most profitable companies in history have to borrow to stay in the race, what hope is there for everyone else?

Nvidia's deal is one answer. Project finance has long funded infrastructure with high up-front costs, paid down by steady returns over many years: power plants, toll roads, airports. What's new is the attempt to turn compute into an asset class that pension funds and insurers are comfortable owning, the way they already own infrastructure.

The arrangement carries risks. The parallel with infrastructure is imperfect: Energy facilities are built to last decades, usually in response to foreseeable demand, and generate predictable returns. In contrast, graphics processing units (GPUs) are short-lived assets; AI demand is unpredictable; and it is too early to project returns.

Still, if the upsides from AI are speculative, so are the downsides—and if the model works, it could reshape the AI market much as venture capital changed the risk calculus for starting a business.

Nvidia's announcement came with familiar worries about circular financing, in which the chipmaker's money comes back to it as chip orders. But this arrangement is the opposite. Nvidia will not, for the most part, be lending its own money—nor will its six partners. The capital comes from third parties: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, household savings. Rather than a closed loop, the buildout is being wired into the wider financial system: the deal does not artificially boost demand but restructures the cost of supply f

Whoever can raise capital cheaply and at scale will set the pace, and that race still favors the United States, whose capital markets are deeper than anyone else's. item.title: The $40-A-Barrel Cost Most Oil Consumers Never See
item.author: Desconocido
item.description:
The $40-A-Barrel Cost Most Oil Consumers Never See
2026-10-19
Por Desconocido
https://www.forbes.com/sites/rrapier/2026/10/18/the-40-a-barrel-cost-most-oil-consumers-never-see/
A photograph taken on October 15, 2026 shows the Russian shadow fleet oil tanker DF PEAK escorted by the French Navy towards La Possession bay, off the coast of the French Indian Ocean island of La Reunion. In anticipation of its arrival, the Prefect of La Reunion issued two orders on October 14, 2026 prohibiting all maritime activities in the area surrounding the vessel. (Photo by Richard BOUHET / AFP via Getty Images)
AFP via Getty Images
When Americans think about the price of oil, they usually focus on the number quoted every day in financial markets. If Brent crude is trading above $100 a barrel or West Texas Intermediate is near $100, those numbers become shorthand for whether oil is expensive or cheap. But that market price is only part of what ultimately determines the cost of getting crude oil to a refinery.
But transportation has become a cost that has become impossible to ignore.
Reuters recently reported
that shipping roughly 2 million barrels of crude from the United States to Japan aboard a very large crude carrier could cost about $81 million. That works out to approximately $40.50 for every barrel on the ship, compared with roughly $9 million for a similar voyage a year earlier. At current rates, freight alone can represent a huge addition to the underlying value of the oil.
For most consumers, tanker rates are an obscure corner of the energy market. Yet the extraordinary increase in shipping costs is helping reshape global oil flows and adding another layer of expense to a market already dealing with elevated crude prices, refinery constraints, and geopolitical risk.
Oil Has to Get to the Refinery
A barrel of crude oil is only useful if it can get from where it is produced to a refinery capable of processing it. The gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products produced there then have to make another journey to the markets where they are consumed.
In normal times, ocean transportation is inexpensive enough on a per-barrel basis that few consumers ever think about it. The largest crude carriers can move roughly 2 million barrels at a time, creating enormous economies of scale and allowing oil to travel halfway around the world without freight overwhelming the value of the cargo.
That system becomes far more expensive when tankers are scarce or voyages become riskier and longer.
The Energy Information Administration says
tanker rates reached record levels in September as insurance costs increased and ships took longer routes to avoid conflict zones. Longer voyages also tie vessels up for more days, effectively reducing the available tanker fleet even if the physical number of ships has not changed.
The distinction between the quoted price of crude and its delivered cost is therefore crucial. A refinery does not care only what a barrel costs at an export terminal. Freight, insurance, delays, and other transportation costs all become part of the economics by the time that barrel arrives.
A Global Transportation Bottleneck
The current tanker crunch developed as geopolitical tensions disrupted traditional oil-trading patterns. Attacks on shipping, higher insurance premiums, changes in routing, and additional ship-to-ship transfers have all absorbed transportation capacity. At the same time, strong demand for vessels on several major routes has pushed charter rates to extraordinary levels.
The impact is already visible in where oil is moving.
Reuters reported
that freight costs from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia recently reached roughly $80 million per cargo, making some U.S. crude uneconomic for Asian refiners. Buyers that might otherwise have purchased American barrels have been looking instead to Middle Eastern or Latin American suppliers simply because the transportation arithmetic changed.
That same freight squeeze
[Transcripcion recortada]

AFP via Getty Images

But that market price is only part of what ultimately determines the cost of getting crude oil to a refinery.

But transportation has become a cost that has become impossible to ignore.

that shipping roughly 2 million barrels of crude from the United States to Japan aboard a very large crude carrier could cost about $81 million. At current rates, freight alone can represent a huge addition to the underlying value of the oil.

For most consumers, tanker rates are an obscure corner of the energy market. Yet the extraordinary increase in shipping costs is helping reshape global oil flows and adding another layer of expense to a market already dealing with elevated crude prices, refinery constraints, and geopolitical risk.

A barrel of crude oil is only useful if it can get from where it is produced to a refinery capable of processing it. The gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products produced there then have to make another journey to the markets where they are consumed.

The largest crude carriers can move roughly 2 million barrels at a time, creating enormous economies of scale and allowing oil to travel halfway around the world without freight overwhelming the value of the cargo.

That system becomes far more expensive when tankers are scarce or voyages become riskier and longer.

The Energy Information Administration says

tanker rates reached record levels in September as insurance costs increased and ships took longer routes to avoid conflict zones. Longer voyages also tie vessels up for more days, effectively reducing the available tanker fleet even if the physical number of ships has not changed.

The distinction between the quoted price of crude and its delivered cost is therefore crucial. A refinery does not care only what a barrel costs at an export terminal. Freight, insurance, delays, and other transportation costs all become part of the economics by the time that barrel arrives.

A Global Transportation Bottleneck

The current tanker crunch developed as geopolitical tensions disrupted traditional oil-trading patterns. Attacks on shipping, higher insurance premiums, changes in routing, and additional ship-to-ship transfers have all absorbed transportation capacity. At the same time, strong demand for vessels on several major routes has pushed charter rates to extraordinary levels.

The impact is already visible in where oil is moving.

Reuters reported

that freight costs from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia recently reached roughly $80 million per cargo, making some U.S. crude uneconomic for Asian refiners. Buyers that might otherwise have purchased American barrels have been looking instead to Middle Eastern or Latin American suppliers simply because the transportation arithmetic changed.

item.title: Meta is 'back on offense,' BofA says — with only one top risk
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Meta is 'back on offense,' BofA says — with only one top risk
2026-10-19
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/meta-is-back-on-offense-bofa-says--with-only-one-top-risk-100000520.html
What a turn of events for Mark Zuckerberg. The Meta CEO has steered his company from an AI also-ran to a leading contender, backed by a seemingly unstoppable ads machine. Fresh off successful debuts of AI agent Muse and a new frontier model, the social giant has won praise from early adopters and analysts who see more upside on a stock that's up close to 10% for the year.
Meta (META) is "back on offense with AI," Bank of America analysts, led by Justin Post, summed up the company's glow-up, which has culminated in a suite of new AI products, in a note on Friday. "Recent AI launches have strengthened confidence in company's AI execution and we see Meta with least risk of AI disruption to core business in our coverage."
The offense is so good it doesn't have to play defense — does it get better than that?
Post's commentary is noteworthy for that enthusiasm. But it also highlights the broader risk for Meta and its peers as it gets set to report quarterly results on Wednesday. Even though its path to full monetization seems ever-clearer, an unexpected jolt upward in AI build-out expenses is still the chief concern.
"[The] top risk is 2027 [earnings per share] pressure on more AI investment," Post wrote.
Unlike the powerhouse AI labs, or Google's (GOOG) deep research background, Meta had been, until fairly recently, viewed as an AI laggard. Microsoft (MSFT) had its partnership with OpenAI, Amazon (AMZN) had its AWS infrastructure, and even Elon Musk's former startup xAI — now part of SpaceX (SPCX) — attracted a certain type of phenom engineer aligned with his worldview.
That line of criticism has clearly given way to bullish sentiment. The AI restructuring and personnel shakeups appear to be paying off.
Post wrote that traction with Muse and its models can drive up Meta's earnings multiple. Zuckerberg's next leg upward, he said, would be propelled by more usage, enterprise deals following Muse Wonder, and the launch of an enterprise coding agent.
All the while, Meta has a humming ads machine, for which its higher-performing models can enhance the content recommendations and ad targeting at the core of its business.
This cash-flow advantage is key to Meta's position in the AI marketplace, as not every AI company is diversified. But like nearly all these companies, a surprise surge in spending expectations, which are already massive, could cause problems for Meta's investor relations.

item.title: Is Anthropic worth $2 trillion? How about $1.5 trillion?
item.author: Michael B Kelley
item.description:
Is Anthropic worth $2 trillion? How about $1.5 trillion?
2026-10-19
Por Michael B Kelley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/is-anthropic-worth-2-trillion-how-about-15-trillion-192500921.html
Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) work will contribute to massive changes in the US economy and workforce, but how much is the leading AI lab actually worth as a public company?
Reuters, citing several people familiar with the matter, reported that current and prospective investors in Anthropic's initial public offering who attended an investor day at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters this week discussed a valuation of the Claude maker at about $1.5 trillion, down from earlier expectations of $2 trillion.
"What's $500 billion between friends in the AI trade?" Yahoo Finance's Jake Conley quipped (video above) before adding, "It does get to the point of you're trying to justify these huge valuations: Do your numbers justify it?"
Anthropic's third quarter revenue reportedly rose 45% from the second quarter to $16.8 billion, and the company stayed profitable on an adjusted basis. Reuters, which got its hands on Anthropic's IPO prospectus, previously reported that revenue more than doubled in the second quarter, to $11.6 billion from $4.7 billion.
"While those numbers assuaged some concerns about the massive costs of developing AI systems," Reuters reported, "some investors were disappointed by the slowing sequential growth rate in the latest quarter."
Yahoo Finance co-host Julie Hyman called the lower price "a reading-the-room moment," with AI stocks selling off this week. "All of this would seem to indicate that there's at least enough concern out there that you're not going to go out and try and overprice."
Hyman also noted that one quarter may not settle it: "We don't know if it's going to reaccelerate in the fourth quarter."
Conley wants a different yardstick than annual recurring revenue (ARR), the run-rate figure AI companies like to cite.
"ARR, that's not a real number," he said. "Give me some GAAP numbers."

item.title: ‘Just another scare’: Wall Street sees the AI trade in tact despite tech's latest rout
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
‘Just another scare’: Wall Street sees the AI trade in tact despite tech's latest rout
2026-10-19
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/just-another-scare-wall-street-sees-the-ai-trade-strong-despite-techs-latest-rout-155930040.html
Technology (XLK) took a hit this week as financing concerns mounted, dragging down key AI trade players and sending the S&P 500 (^GSPC) and Nasdaq (^IXIC) into negative territory for the week.
CoreWeave (CRWV) and peer Nebius (NBIS) both closed out the week down more than 25%. Those companies along with Oracle (ORCL) are "probably at the bottom" of tech on free cash flow, noted Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson on Yahoo Finance last week.
CoreWeave rose 1%, Nebius 3% and Oracle 1% in premarket trading on Monday.
Mortonson pointed to "a higher cost of capital" and "a lot of scrutiny now on circular finance."
Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang sought to ease concerns, expressing optimism about CoreWeave. Nvidia's backing is significant, given that the AI chip giant holds roughly a 10% stake in the neocloud provider.
Others on Wall Street echoed the sentiment.

item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Moderna stock sinks as Wall Street turns cautious following blistering rally
2026-10-17
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/moderna-stock-sinks-as-wall-street-turns-cautious-following-blistering-rally-152233829.html
What happened: Moderna (MRNA) stock tanked 9% on Friday.
What's behind the move: The biotech giant sank as investors took profits and Wall Street grew cautious on the stock's blistering rally of more than 600% year to date.
Goldman Sachs (GS) raised its target on the stock to $137 from $120 on Thursday while maintaining a Neutral rating, implying a more than 40% drop from current levels.
Morgan Stanley (MS) also has a Neutral rating, with a price target of $95. Meanwhile, Citi (C) analysts set an $80 target and a Sell rating on the stock last month, given its rapid run this year.
Wall Street is mostly neutral on the stock with 16 Hold, 5 Buys, and 4 Sell ratings.
What else you need to know: Shares of the biotech company rallied this year as the company is no longer valued solely on its declining COVID-19 vaccine business, but increasingly on its potential to become a major player in cancer treatment.
In August, Moderna announced positive Phase 3 results for its personalized cancer vaccine, developed in partnership with Merck (MRK), helping drive a sharp rally in the stock.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: Memory stocks slide into another bear market as chip losses near $2.5 trillion: Chart of the Day
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
Memory stocks slide into another bear market as chip losses near $2.5 trillion: Chart of the Day
2026-10-17
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/memory-stocks-slide-into-another-bear-market-as-chip-losses-near-25-trillion-chart-of-the-day-100000060.html
AI's appetite for memory keeps growing while investors' appetite for memory stocks is shrinking.
The Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) entered another bear market this week, falling more than 20% from its September rebound high. Losses deepened Thursday, leaving the fund roughly 22% below that peak and nearly 40% below June's record close.
It's been an expensive round trip. DRAM plunged nearly 45% from June to late July, then rallied over 40% into September. The latest selling has erased more than three-quarters of that recovery.
The dollar losses are enormous.
Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), Micron (MU), SK Hynix (SKHY) and Sandisk (SNDK) — all DRAM components — have shed more than $700 billion in combined market value since October 6. A broader Yahoo Finance basket of 61 semiconductor and storage stocks has lost nearly $2.5 trillion.
Samsung plunged nearly 10% Thursday in Seoul, before US trading began. The subsequent US rebound helped Micron finish nearly 2% higher, but the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) still posted its eighth straight decline — its longest losing streak since October 2008.
Strong demand hasn't stopped investors from questioning future profits.
China's CXMT (688825.SS) has announced progress on a denser memory-chip design, raising concerns about competition and pricing power. Yet the challenger fell, too — over 5% Thursday, leaving it down roughly 20% since September's end. DRAM holds it as well, with roughly 5% exposure as of September 30.
Meanwhile, chipmakers helping finance their customers are attracting more scrutiny. That doesn't mean AI demand has disappeared. TSMC (TSM) reported another record quarterly profit Thursday. Investors are questioning how much of the boom will reach shareholders.
DRAM's next major test sits around its late-July lows near $45 — another 9% below Thursday's close. Holding there would preserve the summer trading range. A sustained break would erase the rebound entirely.

item.title: Why CoreWeave, Nebius, and other neocloud stocks are being pounded: Goldman Sachs explains
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Why CoreWeave, Nebius, and other neocloud stocks are being pounded: Goldman Sachs explains
2026-10-17
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/why-coreweave-nebius-and-other-neocloud-stocks-are-being-pounded-goldman-sachs-explains-125730269.html
Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS) are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.
CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are both down about 15% just in the past five days.
While concerns about CoreWeave's financial health are being blamed for the neocloud stock routs, the reality is that it's not just a CoreWeave issue. The overall financial health of the AI economic system build-out is being more closely scrutinized in a land of higher-for-longer interest rates.
Goldman Sachs explained the pressure quite well in a new note on Friday.
US dollar high-yield AI-related debt spreads widened by 25 basis points between Oct. 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360 basis points over Treasurys. By contrast, non-AI-related debt spreads were only two basis points wider and remain below their March peak, Goldman Sachs pointed out (see charts below).
Within AI-related debt issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance.
"While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate," Goldman Sachs strategist Amanda Lynam explained. "Further removed AI-adjacent Energy and Utilities have been more resilient, in our view partly reflecting more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile. We think the widening reflects a reassessment of the economics of the AI buildout, particularly for lower-rated borrowers that are more exposed to higher-for-longer rates and potential energy-cost pressures."
Lynam sees "some near-term reversal" of the recent sell-off in US high-yield debt tied to AI. But she acknowledges that "dispersion across AI-related issuers is likely to remain high."

item.title: From e-cigarettes to abortion rights: A look at how big banks made debanking calls
item.author: David Hollerith
item.description:
From e-cigarettes to abortion rights: A look at how big banks made debanking calls
2026-10-17
Por David Hollerith
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/from-e-cigarettes-to-abortion-rights-a-look-at-how-big-banks-made-debanking-calls-151436497.html
A merchant selling MAGA gear, a religious nonprofit with public views on same-sex marriage, and an abortion rights group whose political donations went overwhelmingly to Democrats.
These were some of the current and prospective customers that the nation's largest banks denied services to, according to a report released this week that offers more details on how political and religious views influenced banks' risk assessments behind closed doors.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which reviewed roughly 50,000 documents from nine large US banks, found that lenders sometimes relied on reputational concerns rather than outright financial risks when deciding whom to bank. Regulators said a range of industries were targeted, including oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms manufacturing, detention facilities, and tobacco and e-cigarette retailers.
The report shed further light on how those decisions played out, including disrupting a religious nonprofit's fundraising process and eliminating a merchant's access to payment services.
The OCC stopped short of determining that the individual cases violated federal law. Federal protections against political discrimination in banking vary.
In the months following the Jan. 6 Capitol riots in 2021, a payments processor owned by JPMorgan Chase closed the accounts of two different merchants selling Donald Trump and MAGA gear after concluding that the products promoted hate, violence, or racial intolerance.
Months later, it did the same to another payments processor after the event organizer "called President Biden and Dr. Anthony Fauci 'the enemy' and characterized Black Lives Matter as Marxists" on social media. Employees for WePay and JPMorgan decided the posts were an "incitement of hate," according to the report.
"[T]here is no set criteria to indicate if A, B, or C word is found to be considered as hate or racism or terrorism, etc," a JPMorgan risk employee later noted. The account closure was ultimately reversed.
A JPMorgan spokesperson said the process used by WePay, a payments technology company it acquired and has since shut down, "did not meet our expectations."
"We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates," the bank said in a statement, adding that its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and that the report highlighted "a limited number of historical interactions among the nearly 90 million customers and small businesses we serve."
While the OCC's findings offer more examples of conservatives encountering so-called debanking issues, the report also highlights that those difficulties weren't exclusive to right-wingers.
Until 2025, one of the business lines of credit card giant Capital One treated any business engaged in "partisan activity" as posing a high reputational risk.
In 2023, Capital One's business line declined a banking relationship with an organization promoting reproductive rights, with an employee noting "it's become so synonymous with abortion and the Dems." Capital One also rejected a gun-rights organization over concerns that customers might interpret the relationship as an endorsement of its political positions.
Capital One has not responded for comment as of this writing.
Wells Fargo asked one of its payment processors to look into a religious nonprofit to be sure it wasn't "associated with products or services that promote hate, violence, harassment, or abuse," according to the report.
Wells Fargo shared information on a third-party website that highlighted the nonprofit's views on same-sex marriage. The payment processor ultimately terminated the nonprofit's account, disrupting its ability to collect donations.
W
[Transcripcion recortada]

"[T]here is no set criteria to indicate if A, B, or C word is found to be considered as hate or racism or terrorism, etc," a JPMorgan risk employee later noted. The account closure was ultimately reversed.

A JPMorgan spokesperson said the process used by WePay, a payments technology company it acquired and has since shut down, "did not meet our expectations."

"We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates," the bank said in a statement, adding that its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and that the report highlighted "a limited number of historical interactions among the nearly 90 million customers and small businesses we serve."

While the OCC's findings offer more examples of conservatives encountering so-called debanking issues, the report also highlights that those difficulties weren't exclusive to right-wingers.

Until 2025, one of the business lines of credit card giant Capital One treated any business engaged in "partisan activity" as posing a high reputational risk.

In 2023, Capital One's business line declined a banking relationship with an organization promoting reproductive rights, with an employee noting "it's become so synonymous with abortion and the Dems." Capital One also rejected a gun-rights organization over concerns that customers might interpret the relationship as an endorsement of its political positions.

Capital One has not responded for comment as of this writing.

Wells Fargo asked one of its payment processors to look into a religious nonprofit to be sure it wasn't "associated with products or services that promote hate, violence, harassment, or abuse," according to the report.

Wells Fargo shared information on a third-party website that highlighted the nonprofit's views on same-sex marriage. The payment processor ultimately terminated the nonprofit's account, disrupting its ability to collect donations.

W

item.title: PepsiCo just lost KFC to Coca-Cola. Here's how much it could sting financially.
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
PepsiCo just lost KFC to Coca-Cola. Here's how much it could sting financially.
2026-10-17
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/pepsico-just-lost-kfc-to-coca-cola-heres-how-much-it-could-sting-financially-123341713.html
This has shaped up to be a year of big losses for beverage and snack giant PepsiCo (PEP).
A double-digit percentage drop in the stock so far this year. Lost sales in the core soda business to rival Coca-Cola (KO). Lost profits because of execution missteps and inflation (see the recent full-year earnings guidance cut).
And the losses look to keep piling up, with the latest one being a really tough one to swallow for longtime PepsiCo and Yum! Brands (YUM) followers — and probably a legion of former execs, such as former legendary PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi and her equally legendary former counterpart at Yum! Brands, David Novak.
The Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday that Yum! Brands-owned KFC struck a deal with Coca-Cola to be its beverage provider for thousands of US restaurants. The deal will reportedly begin in January. PepsiCo will reportedly still supply KFC internationally.
Note that in April, Coca-Cola won the Marriott (MAR) business from PepsiCo.
But the fast food loss stings more.
Yum! Brands spun off from PepsiCo in 1997 under the original name of Tricon Global Restaurants. It changed its name to Yum! Brands in 2002.
The spin-off included PepsiCo's fast food restaurant division: KFC, Pizza Hut, and Taco Bell. The business relationship between the two companies has long been seen as a sacred bond, apparently until now.
"Overall, the move underscores Coca-Cola's strong brand equity as well as a relative brand equity gap vs. PepsiCo," Evercore ISI analyst Robert Ottenstein said. "We believe that this announcement, in some ways, is more notable as QSRs, more so than hotel chains, use beverages as a key driver of traffic."
Ottenstein's analysis shows the lost revenue to PepsiCo could be about $50 million, "which suggests that the retail revenue is closer to ~$350-400 million."

item.title: CoreWeave’s rebound is getting tested — here are the levels bulls need to hold
item.author: Jared Blikre
item.description:
CoreWeave’s rebound is getting tested — here are the levels bulls need to hold
2026-10-17
Por Jared Blikre
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/coreweaves-rebound-is-getting-tested--here-are-the-levels-bulls-need-to-hold-150124017.html
CoreWeave (CRWV) sprang a bear trap Thursday. Now another sell-off is testing whether the bulls can hold their ground.
The AI cloud provider's shares are falling Friday after staging a dramatic reversal the previous session. Shares briefly broke below their summer floor near $60 on Thursday, sank to $59.51, then climbed to $69.76 — a 17% rebound from the low.
That's a classic bear trap: a break below support that reverses, catching traders who bet on further declines. CoreWeave finished Thursday nearly 6% higher, following Wednesday's 15% plunge.
Today's retreat is testing how much of that recovery buyers can defend.
The immediate level to watch is $63.43. That represents a 61.8% Fibonacci retracement of Thursday's advance from $59.51 to $69.76 — a proportion technicians watch for potential support after a rally.
CoreWeave came within roughly $0.21 of that level this morning, reaching $63.64 before recovering some ground. Around $64, the stock has given back more than half of Thursday's rebound.
The financing debate is proving harder to reverse
Thursday's recovery followed reassuring comments from Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is both a major shareholder and a supplier to CoreWeave. As Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferré reported Friday morning, Huang said CoreWeave's strength was improving, and its cost of capital was declining.
BofA Securities senior software analyst Tal Liani is also standing by the company, maintaining a Buy rating and $140 price target.
"First of all, this is more sentiment-driven. This is not about fundamentals," Liani told Yahoo Finance Thursday.
His argument rests on long customer contracts, revenue visibility, and financing supported by those agreements. But confidence in the company's ability to deliver remains far from unanimous. As Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban reported Friday, Bernstein is maintaining an Underperform rating and questioning the economics of its long-term business model.
American Ingenuity Fund portfolio manager Adam Johnson, who disclosed buying more CoreWeave stock Thursday, explained on Yahoo Finance Friday that falling bond prices don't change the interest rate the company agreed to pay on its existing fixed-rate debt. The concern is what CoreWeave will have to pay when it borrows again.
Those financing concerns extend beyond CoreWeave
Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi reported Friday that investors demanded an additional 25 basis points of compensation over Treasurys to hold AI-related high-yield debt between Oct. 13 and Oct. 14. The comparable increase outside AI was just 2 basis points, according to Goldman Sachs.

item.title: The US federal budget deficit for 2026 just came in. It’s $1.992 trillion.
item.author: Ben Werschkul
item.description:
The US federal budget deficit for 2026 just came in. It’s $1.992 trillion.
2026-10-17
Por Ben Werschkul
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/the-us-federal-budget-deficit-for-2026-just-came-in-its-1992-trillion-191917669.html
The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink.
This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion.
The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit.
These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar.
The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion.
The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02.
Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally
The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory.
The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security, but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget.
Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months.
Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits.
A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years.

item.title: Netflix stock falls as executive shake-up aims to revive viewership growth
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Netflix stock falls as executive shake-up aims to revive viewership growth
2026-10-16
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/netflix-stock-falls-as-executive-shake-up-aims-to-revive-viewership-growth-135228949.html
Netflix (NFLX) stock fell in early trading on Friday after the streaming giant announced a leadership shake-up amid slowing viewer engagement.
Former Disney executive Peter Rice was named as Netflix's next chief content officer, replacing Bela Bajaria, who is departing after nearly a decade at the streamer.
The move comes ahead of the company's quarterly results next week as it seeks to reinvigorate viewership growth and strengthen its content amid intensifying competition.
Earlier this week, Netflix said it will cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.
The changes at the streaming giant come amid a generational shift that is reshaping viewing habits, with audiences increasingly moving away from traditional television sets toward mobile devices, noted Piper Sandler director and senior research analyst Tom Champion.
Netflix is expected to report quarterly results next Tuesday, Oct. 20, after the market close.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

Former Disney executive Peter Rice was named as Netflix's next chief content officer, replacing Bela Bajaria, who is departing after nearly a decade at the streamer.
The move comes ahead of the company's quarterly results next week as it seeks to reinvigorate viewership growth and strengthen its content amid intensifying competition.
Earlier this week, Netflix said it will cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.
The changes at the streaming giant come amid a generational shift that is reshaping viewing habits, with audiences increasingly moving away from traditional television sets toward mobile devices, noted Piper Sandler director and senior research analyst Tom Champion.
Netflix is expected to report quarterly results next Tuesday, Oct. 20, after the market close.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.
