item.title: The Upside of Surging Bond Yields
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
The Upside of Surging Bond Yields
2026-10-16
Por Texto propio
The Upside of Surging Bond Yields
morganstanley.com
Key Takeaways
The yield surge looks less like an inflation scare and more like a response to stronger growth, heavier borrowing and shifting Treasury demand.
Stocks have held up as earnings forecasts improve, though market leadership remains concentrated in AI-related technology companies.
The bond selloff may have gone too far—and if rates decline, today’s higher yields may offer both meaningful income and potential price gains.
For investors, a quality-focused approach may favor municipal bonds and large-company stocks with durable, achievable earnings growth.
Bond yields are flashing a message that investors can’t ignore. The 10-year Treasury yield recently hit a 24-year high of 5.3%, amid heavy volatility in fixed-income markets, raising a critical question: Is this a warning sign or an opportunity?
When yields rise, investors often see it as a harbinger of resurgent inflation. However, Morgan Stanley’s Global Investment Committee believes the yield surge is not mainly an inflation scare. Instead, it reflects stronger growth, heavier borrowing and shifting demand for bonds—forces that may have pushed up yields further than fundamentals justify.
That matters for portfolios. Higher yields can now offer compelling income, and if they decline as Morgan Stanley expects, high-quality bonds could also deliver price gains. Select stocks may benefit too, provided earnings keep improving.
Here’s how investors may want to think about the move.
Why Have Yields Been Surging?
Stable inflation expectations suggest price pressures are not the main reason yields have risen. Instead, investors appear to be responding to a mix of stronger U.S. growth, increased borrowing needs and a changing buyer base for Treasuries.
Growth has been more resilient than many expected, supported by investment in artificial intelligence, manufacturing and supply-chain resilience, as well as steady consumer spending. Stronger growth expectations can push rates higher even when inflation expectations remain contained.
At the same time, more debt issuance from governments and companies, including technology firms funding AI infrastructure, means bonds may need to offer higher yields to attract buyers.
A less supportive Fed may also be playing a role, as Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has signaled a move away from large-scale bond purchases and extensive forward guidance—tools that helped suppress long-term rates.
Demand is also shifting toward more price-sensitive private investors, who typically require higher yields when supply rises or uncertainty increases.
How Have Rising Rates Affected U.S. Stocks?
As surging yields roil bond markets, they can also weigh on stocks by raising companies’ financing costs, making bonds more competitive with equities and reducing how much investors are willing to pay for future profit growth.
That pressure has not been felt evenly: Megacap technology stocks, along with software and semiconductor companies tied to AI, have helped support the broader market, while financials, value stocks and small-cap stocks have lagged.
Even so, headline indexes have largely taken the rate surge in stride, helped by continued optimism about corporate profits. Analysts now expect S&P 500 companies to earn between $415 and $420 per share in 2027, a substantial 12% increase in their forecast since the start of the year. With earnings forecasts rising even as higher rates pressure valuations, the S&P 500’s forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen from about 22.5 at the start of the year to roughly 19—leaving parts of the stock market looking more attractively priced.
What Could Higher Yields Mean for Your Portfolio?
Morgan Stanley’s Global Investment Committee sees opportunities in both bonds and stocks, with an emphasis on quality, income and selectivity.
Bonds: We believe the bond selloff has gone too far
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: The 2300 Billion Tokenization Race
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
The 2300 Billion Tokenization Race
2026-10-16
Por Texto propio
The $2.3 Trillion Tokenization Race
morganstanley.com
Key Takeaways
Much of wealth and asset management’s recent expansion has come from rising markets rather than new client money, making it more important to win new business.
Global AUM reached a record $159 trillion in 2025 and is projected to grow by an average of 9% annually through 2030; household financial wealth could expand 7% per year.
How firms use AI and tokenization is likely to separate winners from laggards in the industry's next phase of growth.
Tokenized real-world assets total roughly $40 billion today and are expected to reach $2.3 trillion by 2030.
Asset and wealth managers may increasingly compete on differentiated products, distribution, client relationships, advisor capacity and the ability to grow without costs rising as fast.
The asset and wealth management industry faces a growth challenge: Much of its recent expansion has come from rising markets and currency swings rather than new client money. At the same time, fees remain under pressure, while industry profits are increasingly concentrated in a narrow set of products, sales channels and capabilities.
Leaders in the next phase of growth will likely be firms that offer differentiated products, sharpen distribution, deepen client relationships, expand advisor capacity and scale without costs rising in step, according to a joint report from Morgan Stanley Research and consulting firm Oliver Wyman. The analysis draws on industry data and more than 15 interviews with senior executives at firms managing more than $45 trillion in combined assets under management.
“We see two technology shifts—artificial intelligence and tokenization—widening the gap between winners and laggards,” says Michael Cyprys, Head of U.S. Brokers, Asset Managers and Exchanges for Morgan Stanley Research. “The most successful wealth and asset managers will be those that are able to translate a deeper understanding of the major trends shaping the industry into the right strategic bets and operating models that don’t just get them to the head of the pack but allow them to break free entirely.”
Breaking free, Cyprys adds, means having the right mix of products, clients, investment vehicles and the ability to customize.
For asset managers, outgrowing the market will require distinctive investing and deal-sourcing skills, as well as the ability to package those skills into solutions and reach faster-growing sales channels.
Wealth managers will need to win more new business and turn more of their revenue into profit. Successful firms should combine deeper client relationships and stronger inflows of new client assets with greater advisor capacity and a business model that can grow without costs rising as fast.
A Strong Growth Outlook, With a Catch
Asset and wealth managers entered 2026 at record levels. Global assets under management (AUM) rose 15% in 2025 to $159 trillion, while household financial wealth increased 8.2% to $341 trillion. Morgan Stanley Research and Oliver Wyman expect AUM to grow by an average of 9% annually through 2030, with household financial wealth increasing by an average of 7% annually.
Despite the strong projected growth, success will increasingly depend on how well firms use AI and tokenization.
Financial services firms already use AI, but the analysis suggests that leading firms will distinguish themselves by turning productivity gains into higher revenue and wider profit margins.
“Doing so could require a fundamental reset of how businesses are run and organized, with AI embedded in repeatable workflows built on proprietary data and expertise,” says Betsy Graseck, Morgan Stanley’s Global Head of Banks and Diversified Finance Research.
Tokenization, meanwhile, is moving from experimentation toward real-world utility.
“Firms that focus on products where digital rails address clear client needs—particularly in cash management,

item.title: Walmart stock moves higher after Deutsche Bank upgrades to Buy, raises price target
item.author: Brooke DiPalma
item.description:
Walmart stock moves higher after Deutsche Bank upgrades to Buy, raises price target
2026-10-16
Por Brooke DiPalma
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/walmart-stock-moves-higher-after-deutsche-bank-upgrades-to-buy-raises-price-target-135455981.html
In an ongoing inflationary environment, Walmart (WMT) is poised to win, according to Deutsche Bank analyst Krisztina Katai, who upgraded the stock to a Buy rating from Neutral on Thursday morning.
"We believe the current inflationary environment should reinforce Walmart's value proposition and support accelerated share gains, while we think investors are starting to increasingly look beyond the headline pressure on U.S. comp.," Katai wrote in a note to clients.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' September Consumer Price Index, overall inflation rose 3.7% in September, an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Grocery prices increased by 1.8%, but were roughly flat month over month.
Walmart stock popped 3% in premarket trading.
In the second quarter, the company posted its slowest US same-store sales growth since Q4 of 2020, at 2.6%.
Katai said in a meeting with CFO John David Rainey that the company noted consumer trends were stable to improving compared to three months ago, while price gaps remain strong compared to its competitors.
Grocery still accounts for the majority of Walmart's US sales, but general merchandise, including apparel, represents a growing part of the business, and the percentage of sales coming from private-label brands increased by 1.3 percentage points year over year.
That momentum seems to be holding, with strong gains in food, e-commerce, and its marketplace. Higher-profit businesses, like advertising and membership fees, are also expected to boost margins.
As of late, the retail giant has leaned into its fashion offerings with private-label brands Scoop, Free Assembly, and Scenario as part of a bet to attract the deeper wallets of higher-income customers
Brooke DiPalma is a reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

item.title: Car shoppers have had it with price increases
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Car shoppers have had it with price increases
2026-10-16
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/car-shoppers-have-had-it-with-price-increases-100000202.html
More car buyers are exercising their most powerful negotiating tool: walking away.
It probably has something to do with the idea of an $800 car payment, the painful result of near-record prices for new vehicles and stubbornly high interest rates.
Affordability is the key constraint facing publicly traded dealerships, according to Bank of America analysts led by Alexander Perry, in a note on Thursday. In parts and service too, customers are pushing back on pricing and putting off repair work.
Ahead of earnings, BofA is lowering earnings estimates on five major dealers, including Asbury (ABG), AutoNation (AN), and Group 1 (GPI), because of weaker demand for new units and more deferrals on recommended work.
The average transaction price for a new vehicle is now above $50,000, according to a recent analysis by Kelley Blue Book. And it's not just because Americans love their trucks and large SUVs. Two of the most popular, more affordable segments are also driving up the average price. Price increases on subcompact SUVs and compact cars means there is no escape from car inflation.
BofA's survey of 70 dealers found that vehicle pricing was the most cited constraint on new vehicle sales, at 66%. Financing costs came in as the second most popular reason, at 47%. Inflation and high interest rates, clear as day.
More than half of the dealers reported seeing some pushback on pricing as customers delayed work. And another 11% of dealers said they are losing repair orders altogether as customers balk at the cost.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/car-shoppers-have-had-it-with-price-increases-100000202.html
More car buyers are exercising their most powerful negotiating tool: walking away.
It probably has something to do with the idea of an $800 car payment, the painful result of near-record prices for new vehicles and stubbornly high interest rates.
Affordability is the key constraint facing publicly traded dealerships, according to Bank of America analysts led by Alexander Perry, in a note on Thursday. In parts and service too, customers are pushing back on pricing and putting off repair work.
Ahead of earnings, BofA is lowering earnings estimates on five major dealers, including Asbury (ABG), AutoNation (AN), and Group 1 (GPI), because of weaker demand for new units and more deferrals on recommended work.
The average transaction price for a new vehicle is now above $50,000, according to a recent analysis by Kelley Blue Book. And it's not just because Americans love their trucks and large SUVs. Two of the most popular, more affordable segments are also driving up the average price. Price increases on subcompact SUVs and compact cars means there is no escape from car inflation.
BofA's survey of 70 dealers found that vehicle pricing was the most cited constraint on new vehicle sales, at 66%. Financing costs came in as the second most popular reason, at 47%. Inflation and high interest rates, clear as day.
More than half of the dealers reported seeing some pushback on pricing as customers delayed work. And another 11% of dealers said they are losing repair orders altogether as customers balk at the cost.

item.title: Wall Street on Alert for Bessent to Act on Bond Yields Again
item.author: Michael MacKenzie; Alexandra Harris
item.description:
Wall Street on Alert for Bessent to Act on Bond Yields Again
2026-10-16
Por Michael MacKenzie; Alexandra Harris
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/wall-street-alert-bessent-act-144545605.html
(Bloomberg) -- Wall Street traders wrong-footed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's surprise August decision to upsize purchases of older securities are game-planning for more activism, with key clues potentially surfacing Friday as the department prepares to update its debt management plans in November.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Bessent's "Treasury twist" came in response to surging US yields, a sore spot for a Trump administration that had promised to deliver lower borrowing costs — and it initially did have an effect. But by intervening as he did, Bessent also effectively tore up the Treasury's decades-long playbook of being "regular and predictable" with its actions to achieve the lowest debt costs over time.
From a high-level perspective, the move sparked debate over whether such tinkering, by injecting uncertainty, might end up making the market more volatile. On a more practical note, though, it put Wall Street on watch for the possibility of further activism at the Treasury's next quarterly debt-refunding announcement in November, just one day after midterm elections.
On Friday, the biggest bond dealers will receive a list of survey questions by the Treasury ahead of the refunding. Market watchers say the nature of the queries may serve as a Rorschach test of Bessent's leanings.
"You've announced to the market that these yield levels are problematic," said Vishal Khanduja, head of broad markets fixed income at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. "That's why we believe that the next two refundings, with November right after the midterms, are going be pivotal."
There are several ways the Treasury could go, said Martin Tobias, a strategist on the banking side at Morgan Stanley. The most conventional option would be a continuation of the status quo: maintaining current auction sizes at least for the next several quarters with no changes to forward guidance, as it did in August. Another alternative would be to revise forward guidance on issuance to exclude increases to the longer-dated securities, while focusing on increases in two- to seven-year maturities.
Yet another option — and least conventional — would be to explicitly state how large the Treasury's share of bills can be. Officials have never articulated how large a slice they're willing to tolerate, even as the share of bill issuance has grown.
For Ed Al-Hussainy, portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle Investments, the best option from a taxpayers' perspective would be to finance the government in the five-year area instead of as long as 30 years.
"If your objective is to stop the movement of yields higher, then you are going to have to get really creative," he said.
A representative for the Treasury didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Market participants see every option as a possibility, with long-term benchmark yields near their highest in decades in the US and globally. The rise has been fueled by higher oil prices and a Federal Reserve resuming rate hikes that reflects economic expansion replete with sticky inflation. There is also global competition for capital as AI hyperscalers borrow heavily to fund their explosive growth.
All of this comes as US annual interest expense has surpassed $1 trillion for the first time on record and debt servicing costs are now bigger than the defense budget, making the job of financing the government that much trickier. Even though Bessent is limited in his ability to significantly bring down borrowing costs, he has said he still has a "big tool kit" at his disposal and signaled he will use whatever means he can to rein in long-term yields.
Wall Street will also get another chance to weigh in when the Treasury and a group of dealers and investors, called the Treasury Borrowing Advisor
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Wall Street is 'tiring of the Bank of Nvidia, the Bank of AMD and the Bank of Broadcom': Baird's Mortonson
item.author: Michael B Kelley
item.description:
Wall Street is 'tiring of the Bank of Nvidia, the Bank of AMD and the Bank of Broadcom': Baird's Mortonson
2026-10-16
Por Michael B Kelley
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/wall-street-is-tiring-of-the-bank-of-nvidia-the-bank-of-amd-and-the-bank-of-broadcom-bairds-mortonson-121235021.html
Wall Street is 'tiring of the Bank of Nvidia, the Bank of AMD and the Bank of Broadcom': Baird's Mortonson
The sell-off in AI-related stocks, according to Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson, is increasingly about who needs financing and what that financing costs.
"I think the street is tiring of the Bank of Nvidia, the Bank of AMD and the Bank of Broadcom," Mortonson told Yahoo Finance Senior Reporter Brooke DiPalma (video above), referring to chipmakers Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO).
"This is very unusual in this cycle… It's not going over well with the institutional community," he added.
Mortonson pointed to "a higher cost of capital" and "a lot of scrutiny now on circular finance," which he said was "coming out of the Anthropic research meeting."
Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) reportedly told investors at a closed meeting that its third-quarter revenue climbed to $16.8 billion.
CoreWeave stock (CRWV) fell more than 15% on Wednesday and fell again in pre-market trading on Thursday. Mortonson noted that that CoreWeave, Nebius (NBIS), and Oracle (ORCL) are "probably at the bottom" of tech on free cash flow.
Read more: Oracle stock falls on more debt to fund AI chip buying, OpenAI revenue disclosure
These companies are "very dependent on financing going forward," he said., adding: "That is the real issue… their free cash flow and the cost of capital [is] so elevated today that anything that has that exposure is being sold."
Adding to the souring sentiment, a new Gartner forecast that most neocloud providers will "cease independent operations" by 2030.
'That's the million dollar question'
Chipmakers with strong results are getting hit, too.
"Portfolio managers are selling names that have unadulterated blowout numbers, and they're not acting well," Mortonson said, pointing to Samsung (005930.KS), Micron (MU), and ASML (ASML).
Read more: Global chip sell-off deepens as South Korean market plunges
So is the drop a chance to buy? "That's the million dollar question," Mortonson said.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) was up about 87% for the year as of Oct. 6, which he called "a good decade of performance." It closed Wednesday up 65% for that period.
The pullback is "healthy," Mortonson said, but it also "represents that the institutional community that has been very overweight the infrastructure play [and] is going elsewhere."
Where? "They're probably going to software, to be honest with you."
Some money is leaving tech altogether, he added, as a lot of portfolio managers "are trying to lock in performance as they go into the end of the year."

item.title: Fed's Goolsbee: Even without AI, the economy would not be in recession
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Fed's Goolsbee: Even without AI, the economy would not be in recession
2026-10-16
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/feds-goolsbee-even-without-ai-the-economy-would-not-be-in-recession-103000277.html
As artificial intelligence develops at a blistering pace, boosting parts of the economy, both industry leaders and watchdogs argue it should be slowed down to ensure the technology is developed safely.
But what would that mean for economic growth? Would the economy be as strong without AI?
Chicago Federal Reserve president Austan Goolsbee argues that the AI boom isn't simply adding to economic growth; it is actively cannibalizing resources from other traditional industries.
"You can't just look at the rest of the economy and say that's how it would be doing if the AI build-out wasn't there," Goolsbee said in an interview with Yahoo Finance. "Part of why I haven't thought until recently that AI was overheating the aggregate economy is that it's kind of uncomfortably shoving down other sectors."
Goolsbee said he's seeing this play out in his Midwestern district, where local businesses are increasingly complaining about skyrocketing costs, driven directly by intense competition with tech giants.
"A lot of it is we're in competition for the same resources, the same electricians, the same components, the same land, the same construction," Goolsbee said.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
Since AI's rise has suppressed other sectors, the aggregate economy has managed to avoid boiling over. A sudden slowdown in AI wouldn't automatically trigger a recession, Goolsbee said, because if tech demand were to cool, it could simply release pent-up capacity and allow sidelined industries to recover.
However, Goolsbee warned that the velocity of the AI build-out is starting to boost growth more widely.
"The growth has been so rapid that now you're starting to see a retightening of the labor market," Goolsbee cautioned. "Now it becomes more of a concern of just the old-fashioned overheated demand kind of variety."

item.title: Wholesale prices bubbled higher in September, keeping a rate hike on the table
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Wholesale prices bubbled higher in September, keeping a rate hike on the table
2026-10-16
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/wholesale-prices-bubbled-higher-in-september-keeping-a-rate-hike-on-the-table-133644620.html
Wholesale prices in September rose to their highest level in nearly four years, largely propelled by higher energy prices. The sharp increase stokes concerns that inflation could broaden and keep the Federal Reserve on watch for further rate hikes.
The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand, which measures the prices that factories, farmers, and producers charge for their finished goods and services, rose 6.3% last month, the largest increase since December 2022. The data trounced expectations for a 5.4% rise.
On a "core" basis, excluding food and energy, PPI jumped 0.7% month over month in September, handily higher than market expectations of 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, this core measure jumped 5.0%, up from 4.7% previously
"With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.
"While we don't expect them to raise rates later this month because it is so close to the mid-term election, we do think that they will increase the Fed Funds rate another 25 bps in December," Zaccarelli added.
Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to gasoline prices, which jumped 20.3%. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7%.
Looking into the supply chain, the increases in the price of goods sold by one business to another were broad-based, with the index for processed goods rising 2.5%, prices for unprocessed goods moving up 8.4%, and the index for services advancing 0.9%.
The index for processed goods sold to other businesses rose 2.5%, the largest rise since jumping 2.8% in May — with most of the increase due to a 10% spike in energy prices. Nearly half of the rise in processed goods sold to other businesses is attributable to a 21% increase in diesel fuel prices.
Wholesale prices act as an early-warning pipeline for inflation. If the prices of these input goods rise, manufacturers could pass those higher costs down to consumers later.
In the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, four districts reported that the pace of price increases has picked up since September. Higher oil prices permeated all 12 Fed districts. Companies reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain.
Businesses in multiple districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance. Consumer-facing companies said their profit margins have tightened as price-sensitive customers continue to resist price hikes. Businesses are managing their margins with selective price hikes, targeted incentives, and menu changes that reduce their costs.
The reading on wholesale prices for September comes a day after consumer prices also surprised to the upside. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September, compared with expectations for 3.6%, and an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Month-over-month prices rose 0.6%, versus expectations for 0.5%. item.content:encoded:
Wholesale prices bubbled higher in September, keeping a rate hike on the table

2026-10-16

Por Jennifer Schonberger

https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/wholesale-prices-bubbled-higher-in-september-keeping-a-rate-hike-on-the-table-133644620.html

Wholesale prices in September rose to their highest level in nearly four years, largely propelled by higher energy prices. The sharp increase stokes concerns that inflation could broaden and keep the Federal Reserve on watch for further rate hikes.

The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand, which measures the prices that factories, farmers, and producers charge for their finished goods and services, rose 6.3% last month, the largest increase since December 2022. The data trounced expectations for a 5.4% rise.

On a "core" basis, excluding food and energy, PPI jumped 0.7% month over month in September, handily higher than market expectations of 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, this core measure jumped 5.0%, up from 4.7% previously

"With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

"While we don't expect them to raise rates later this month because it is so close to the mid-term election, we do think that they will increase the Fed Funds rate another 25 bps in December," Zaccarelli added.

Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to gasoline prices, which jumped 20.3%. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7%.

Looking into the supply chain, the increases in the price of goods sold by one business to another were broad-based, with the index for processed goods rising 2.5%, prices for unprocessed goods moving up 8.4%, and the index for services advancing 0.9%.

The index for processed goods sold to other businesses rose 2.5%, the largest rise since jumping 2.8% in May — with most of the increase due to a 10% spike in energy prices. Nearly half of the rise in processed goods sold to other businesses is attributable to a 21% increase in diesel fuel prices.

Wholesale prices act as an early-warning pipeline for inflation. If the prices of these input goods rise, manufacturers could pass those higher costs down to consumers later.

In the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, four districts reported that the pace of price increases has picked up since September. Higher oil prices permeated all 12 Fed districts. Companies reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain.

Businesses in multiple districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance. Consumer-facing companies said their profit margins have tightened as price-sensitive customers continue to resist price hikes. Businesses are managing their margins with selective price hikes, targeted incentives, and menu changes that reduce their costs.

The reading on wholesale prices for September comes a day after consumer prices also surprised to the upside. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September, compared with expectations for 3.6%, and an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Month-over-month prices rose 0.6%, versus expectations for 0.5%. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%, holding the same level as August. The year-over-year rate was 2.6%, compared with expectations for 2.5%, and up from 2.4% in August.

Analysts will use PPI and CPI to back into the Fed's preferred inflation gauge – the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index. Stephen Brown, an economist at Capital Economics, estimates that core PCE rose 0.35% in September.

"That makes an October rate hike a bit more likely, with the FOMC's decision coming down to developments in broader fin

item.title: TSMC stock drops despite record profit amid 'extremely robust demand' for AI chips
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
TSMC stock drops despite record profit amid 'extremely robust demand' for AI chips
2026-10-16
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/tsmc-stock-drops-despite-record-profit-amid-extremely-robust-demand-for-ai-chips-152649370.html
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSM) shares fell 2% despite strong quarterly results as a sector-wide sell-off weighed on the contract chipmaker.
TSMC reported a sixth straight quarter of record profits, with the company's bottom line jumping nearly 69% while revenue surged 51%.
The Taiwan-based contract chip manufacturer's sales are expected to reach as much as $54.3 billion for its current quarter, beating analyst estimates.
"Demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust," TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said during the call. "We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance."
Third quarter gross margin was 66.4%, down from 67.7% in the second quarter. TSMC expects a gross margin of 65% to 67% for the fourth quarter.
"Given the continued robust multi-year demand from our customers, including the emerging agentic AI market, we reiterate our full-year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion," TSMC CFO Wendell Huang said.
The company expects capital expenditures from 2026 to 2028 "to be even more significantly higher than the past three years," as it continues to invest heavily to support customers' growth, Huang added.
The company is closely tied to the AI infrastructure build-out and its execution, as it manufactures advanced processors designed by chip giants such as Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO).
TSMC stock is up more than 41% year to date as of Wednesday's close. Shares reached all-time highs earlier this month after Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) CEO Elon Musk acknowledged early-stage talks with the world's largest chip foundry about a potential collaboration on his Terafab semiconductor initiative in Texas.
TSMC, which is already undergoing significant expansion in Arizona as part of a multiyear plan to manufacture chips stateside for its clients, confirmed it is exploring Texas.
"We send the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation," Wei said during the call. "We also talk to one of our customers who try to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: AI trade rout sparks flight to Treasurys, bond yields sink: Chart of the Day
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
AI trade rout sparks flight to Treasurys, bond yields sink: Chart of the Day
2026-10-16
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/ai-trade-rout-sparks-flight-to-treasurys-bond-yields-sink-chart-of-the-day-151821305.html
A sell-off in the AI trade has fueled investor interest in Treasurys, driving dramatic swings in bond yields.
The 10-year Treasury (^TNX) yield, used as a benchmark for mortgages and other loans, sank 14 basis points to 5.05%. The 30-year yield (^TYX) also tumbled 13 basis points to 5.40%, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart below.
A global sell-off in chip stocks, exacerbated by AI financing worries, pushed investors toward Treasurys. Bond yields extended declines after reversing their gains on Wednesday following a hotter-than-expected inflation report.
The two-day action in bond yields could be a precursor to the road ahead if AI spending were to decelerate.
"It would weaken the USD and reduce US yields across the curve," wrote Thierry Wizman, global FX & rates strategist at Macquarie Group.
"That's because it would mark the end of superlative US growth against the rest of the developed economies," he said.
Bond yields have hit the highest levels in more than 20 years, raising concerns about higher borrowing costs and their impact on the broader stock market.
Sticky inflation has also led strategists to price in at least another rate hike this year. However, as of Thursday morning, market participants have raised their probability to 72% that Federal Reserve officials will hold rates steady at their policy meeting this month.
Macquarie Group strategists, along with UBS and Goldman Sachs analysts, see a Fed pause in October, followed by a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting.
Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities. She has reported live from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.
Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocks

item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
TSMC posts record profit amid 'extremely robust demand' for AI chips
2026-10-15
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/tsmc-posts-record-profit-amid-extremely-robust-demand-for-ai-chips-104536579.html
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSM) shares fell 4% as strong quarterly results from the contract chipmaker did little to lift sentiment around the AI trade amid a deepening sector-wide sell-off.
TSMC reported a sixth straight quarter of record profits, with the company's bottom line jumping nearly 69% while revenue surged 51%.
The Taiwan-based contract chip manufacturer's sales are expected to reach as much as $54.3 billion for its current quarter, beating analyst estimates.
"Demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust," TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said during the call. "We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance."
Third quarter gross margin was 66.4%, down from 67.7% in the second quarter. TSMC expects a gross margin of 65% to 67% for the fourth quarter.
"Given the continued robust multi-year demand from our customers, including the emerging agentic AI market, we reiterate our full-year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion," TSMC CFO Wendell Huang said.
The company expects capital expenditures from 2026 to 2028 "to be even more significantly higher than the past three years," as it continues to invest heavily to support customers' growth, Huang added.
The company is closely tied to the AI infrastructure build-out and its execution, as it manufactures advanced processors designed by chip giants such as Nvidia (NVDA), AMD (AMD), and Broadcom (AVGO).
TSMC stock is up more than 41% year to date as of Wednesday's close. Shares reached all-time highs earlier this month after Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) CEO Elon Musk acknowledged early-stage talks with the world's largest chip foundry about a potential collaboration on his Terafab semiconductor initiative in Texas.
TSMC, which is already undergoing significant expansion in Arizona as part of a multiyear plan to manufacture chips stateside for its clients, confirmed it is exploring Texas.
"We send the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation," Wei said during the call. "We also talk to one of our customer who try to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: At its New York design studio, Walmart bets on affordable, trendy clothes
item.author: Brooke DiPalma
item.description:
At its New York design studio, Walmart bets on affordable, trendy clothes
2026-10-15
Por Brooke DiPalma
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/at-its-new-york-design-studio-walmart-bets-on-affordable-trendy-clothes-100000100.html
NEW YORK — On the fifth floor of an unassuming building in Manhattan, Walmart's New York City fashion office buzzes with activity as the low-cost retailer pushes for recognition in one of the style capitals of the world.
The minimalist office, formerly occupied by menswear brand Bonobos, is where Walmart (WMT) designs apparel for its private-label brands Scoop, Free Assembly, and Scenario as part of a betto attract the deeper wallets of higher-income customers.
There, roughly 160 Walmart employees across brand, design, fit, and style teams work to create $60 cashmere sweaters and other trendy items that the company hopes inspire people to ask, "That's from Walmart?!"
"We made a real intentional choice to say that we wanted to move forward even more in our fashion," Walmart US executive vice president and chief merchandising officer Julie Barber told Yahoo Finance. "The majority of our team sits in Bentonville. They're doing the buying, but we needed a select group of people here in New York closer to some of the trends and things that were happening."

item.title: The S&P 500 is about to break its longest streak without a 1% drop
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
The S&P 500 is about to break its longest streak without a 1% drop
2026-10-15
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/the-sp-500-is-about-to-break-its-longest-streak-without-a-1-drop-131750025.html
The stock market keeps on stacking good days only.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) has gone an astonishing 52 trading days without a 1% down day, matching the streak that ended in July 2024, according to research from Global Markets Investor. If the index avoids such a decline in today's session, the streak will become the longest since January 2020, when it lasted 74 trading days.
We say astonishing given the headwinds continuing to be thrown at the market, from elevated inflation to a September interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve to midterm election uncertainty.
No big deal, apparently, as the Teflon market vibes rage on.
Meanwhile, Global Markets Investor noted that the New York Stock Exchange has gone 224 consecutive trading days without a session in which declining stocks accounted for at least 80% of total trading volume, the longest streak since at least 1996.
Looked at another way, the market has gone nearly a year without a day of intense, broad-based selling on the NYSE.
Investors continue to stay long stocks amid a strong earnings outlook.
S&P 500 third quarter earnings growth is expected to come in at 29.6% year over year.
If 29.6% is the actual growth rate for the quarter, it will mark the third straight quarter of growth above 25%, according to FactSet.
It would also represent the eighth straight quarter of double-digit percentage earnings growth.
For the fourth quarter, Wall Street analysts are calling for earnings growth of 28%.
Analysts are predicting year-over-year earnings growth of 32.7% for 2026. Earnings are seen up 15.6% for 2027.

item.title: The advent of superintelligent AI poses 3 big challenges for investors, Deutsche Bank warns
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
The advent of superintelligent AI poses 3 big challenges for investors, Deutsche Bank warns
2026-10-15
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-advent-of-superintelligent-ai-poses-3-big-challenges-for-investors-deutsche-bank-warns-180036873.html
AI models are only getting smarter, and that means the investing game could be about to change in very big ways, analysts at Deutsche Bank warned in a lengthy new white paper released on Tuesday.
"Under our scenario, by 2030 the best performing AI models would have the qualities of 'superintelligence', that is better than human experts in all domains," Deutsche Bank analyst Adrian Cox wrote. "These would be frontier models: and using them would feel exactly like bringing the best human experts in a room to solve whatever business problem you faced. And the equivalents of today's frontier models would be available, quite literally, everywhere, compressed enough to run on every phone, tablet or laptop computer."
Humans are already getting a flavor of what these models can potentially do across sectors like medicine, law, and robotics.
In robotics alone, Cox pointed to recent news from Nvidia (NVDA) as evidence of the power of superintelligence. This past June, Nvidia trained robot arms to seat GPUs and cut zip ties. Under a superintelligence situation, the entire factory could be retooled overnight using robots.
"In early 2026, we already see early examples of what highly capable AI can do," Cox explained. "They give a flavour for a world with superintelligence even if the reality would be a leap beyond, both quantitatively and qualitatively. At that point, superintelligence would mark a regime break, not a faster version of what we already have. Rather than blindly doing what humans specify, but just a bit better, it would specify the task itself."
3 big changes investors should prepare for
Of greatest interest, at least to us, is what Cox writes about future challenges for the average investor posed by superintelligence.
"Diversification normally works because idiosyncratic risks are unrelated and average each other out. Here they would not: with one variable that overrides everything else, spreading capital across more names would just spread exposure rather than diluting it," Cox said.
Consequently, Cox suggested investors may need to consider adapting their approach in three ways.
First, investors should classify investments as adopters or casualties rather than position off averages.
"Under a normal distribution, errors are symmetric and partially cancel each other out," Cox said. "But under bimodality they do not: to put a firm in one category or another means getting it completely right or wrong. Position size should track confidence in the classification."
Second, they should avoid reading calm price action as low risk.

item.title: Federal watchdog says 9 large US banks denied service to customers over political or religious views
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Federal watchdog says 9 large US banks denied service to customers over political or religious views
2026-10-15
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/federal-watchdog-says-9-large-us-banks-denied-service-to-customers-over-political-or-religious-views-160634194.html
Federal watchdog says 9 large US banks denied service to customers over political or religious views
The Comptroller of the Currency says the nation's nine largest banks denied financial services to customers based on their political, religious, or social beliefs, according to a regulatory review released Wednesday.
The OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and received approximately 50,000 documents from JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank regarding their policies, procedures, practices, and individual customer decisions.
The federal banking watchdog determined that the banks' sweeping internal guidelines lacked objective, risk-based criteria, effectively shutting out legitimate customers and businesses based on ideological leanings rather than financial risk.
The OCC said its findings reveal a systematic effort within the banking sector to restrict access for politically sensitive industries through both public and nonpublic policies.
Federal regulators found that lenders restricted certain sectors' access to financial services, including oil and gas exploration; coal mining; firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution; construction or operation of detention facilities; and the manufacturing, distribution or online retail of tobacco or e-cigarettes.
The Trump administration has voiced growing concerns over "de-banking" and the use of the financial system to achieve social and political objectives.
"Today's report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. "
All nine banks report having reassessed the role of reputation risk in decisions to accept or terminate new customers, according to the OCC's report. Several banks said they had minimized reliance on reputation risk, and bank employees now must consider it in the context of other financial or business consequences, including credit risk, money laundering and terrorist financing risk.
The Bank Policy Institute, a lobbying group that represents the banks, said in a statement in reaction to the report, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk."

item.title: Bending Spoons stock soars on new Berkshire Hathaway investment
item.author: Michael B Kelley
item.description:
Bending Spoons stock soars on new Berkshire Hathaway investment
2026-10-15
Por Michael B Kelley
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/bending-spoons-stock-soars-on-new-berkshire-hathaway-investment-151759397.html
Bending Spoons stock (BSP) soared 41% on Wednesday after the Italian tech company said Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-B) will invest another $330 million in it.
The stock rose 54% to $58 per share at one point in the morning, just shy of its intraday record of $58.94 set on Aug. 11. Wednesday was the stock's best day since its July 1 market debut.
Trading volume passed 9.8 million, more than four times the stock's three-month daily average, according to Yahoo Finance data.
Berkshire is buying the new stock in a private placement at $33 per share, about 13% below Tuesday's close, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday.
The deal lifts Berkshire's stake to 4%, the company said. Berkshire invested $600 million in Bending Spoons at its initial public offering in July. The IPO was priced at $29.
The stock is up around 80% from its IPO price, giving Bending Spoons a market value of about $33 billion.
Bending Spoons said it will use the money for general corporate purposes and new acquisitions. It expects the deal to close in the fourth quarter. Neither the announcement nor the filing included a comment from Berkshire.

item.title: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee calls September inflation 'discouraging' but favors waiting on more data
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Chicago Fed's Goolsbee calls September inflation 'discouraging' but favors waiting on more data
2026-10-15
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/chicago-feds-goolsbee-calls-september-inflation-discouraging-but-favors-waiting-on-more-data-185843740.html
Chicago Federal Reserve president Austan Goolsbee called a hotter-than-expected reading on September inflation "discouraging" but suggested that he wants to wait for more data before taking action to raise interest rates higher.
"We need to get more data," Goolsbee said in an interview with Yahoo Finance. "We need to get the through line. If the through line on inflation is this 4% core inflation, then that's not acceptable. That's not compatible with the Fed target, and our policy needs to address that."
That 4%, he said, refers to a projection of September's core price change over a full 12-month period, showing what the annual inflation rate would be if that exact monthly pace kept up for an entire year. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September, compared with expectations for 3.6%, and marking an acceleration from 3.4% in August.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%, holding the same level as August. The year-over-year rate was 2.6%, compared with expectations for 2.5%, and up from 2.4% in August.
"I found it discouraging, and to pile on, last month was also discouraging," Goolsbee said.
He's concerned not just about the overall number but also about services inflation, which he sees showing little sign of improvement, with a reading above 5%. He noted that higher services inflation can't be chalked up to tariffs or higher oil prices. Core goods inflation above 3% should have come down as tariffs made their way through, Goolsbee said, but it hasn't, pointing toward more persistent inflation. He also noted that the AI data center build-out warrants close watch because of its potential to overheat the economy.
On the ground in his Midwestern district, Goolsbee said he's hearing all about costs and prices.
"There's very little that we're hearing that sounds like downturn, risks of recession, and things like that," he said. "So that makes you more nervous about demand side overheating than just straight supply shock."
Asked whether rates are high enough at current levels to bring inflation back down to 2% or whether additional rate hikes are needed, Goolsbee said, "I don't think we yet know the answer to that."
He added, "If we get more months like this … that's totally unacceptable."
Goolsbee noted that he's one of the more "optimistic folks" at the Fed about how much progress can be made on inflation over the next year — but added the caveat that he said in the fall of 2024 that he was uncomfortable with front-loading rate cuts on the premise that inflation would be transitory.

item.title: Social Security announces 3.6% COLA for 2027, the highest in 4 years
item.author: Kerry Hannon
item.description:
Social Security announces 3.6% COLA for 2027, the highest in 4 years
2026-10-15
Por Kerry Hannon
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/social-security-announces-36-cola-for-2027-the-highest-in-4-years-135447865.html
The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027. That's well above both this year's COLA and the 2.6% average over the past two decades.
Starting in January, the increase will add an average of $75 per month for roughly 75 million retired seniors and disabled workers.
The 2027 COLA will be the highest in four years — but still not enough for millions of retirees to keep up with rising food, energy, and healthcare costs.
The COLA is "supposed to offset inflation, but it under-measures it," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance. "Thanks to the war in Iran and the tariffs, we've got raging inflation and the COLA, as important as it is, will not fully offset the inflation seniors are experiencing."
The annual cost-of-living adjustment is many retirees' only source of retirement income that is not subject to inflation risk. That inflation protection is crucial because Social Security is also the largest source of income for many retirees.
Read more: Retirement planning by age: The complete guide for your 20s-70s
Today, for about half of seniors, their monthly Social Security benefit provides at least 50% of their income, and for about 1 in 4, it's at least 90%.
For more than a quarter, it's their only source of income. The average retiree's benefit is $2,087.52 per month and will rise to $2,162.67.
The math behind the hike
The COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for urban workers, or CPI-W, which weights the costs of goods and services paid by the urban segment of the population more than other expense categories. It averages data for July, August, and September, then compares that figure with the same period last year.
Inflation heated up to 3.7% annually last month as energy prices soared, new data showed, driven primarily by higher energy prices.
Critics argue that the index does not accurately reflect the expenses many seniors face.
One proposal would use the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, to calculate COLAs. CPI-E expenditures are weighted differently, with medical care, housing, and recreation costs making up a larger share of the index than food, apparel, transportation, and education costs.
Read more: How to find out your Social Security COLA for 2027
"The CPI-E is designed around the spending patterns of older Americans" and "can provide a more realistic measure of the inflation they experience," said Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, a nonprofit advocacy organization.

item.title: Morgan Stanley’s Wealth Arm Brings in Record New Money From IPOs
item.author: Hannah Levitt; Sridhar Natarajan
item.description:
Morgan Stanley’s Wealth Arm Brings in Record New Money From IPOs
2026-10-15
Por Hannah Levitt; Sridhar Natarajan
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/morgan-stanley-wealth-arm-brings-115105080.html
(Bloomberg) -- Morgan Stanley's profit for the third quarter climbed as the firm's equity traders trounced analysts' estimates and the firm's wealth-management operation brought in a record amount of money.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The stock-trading business generated revenue of $5.8 billion, compared with expectations for $4.9 billion, while the closely watched wealth business soaked up a record $232 billion in net new assets, according to a statement Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley said half of those net new assets were tied to initial public offerings. The firm's IPO bankers have worked on some of the year's biggest listings, including SpaceX. Elon Musk's aerospace company is a customer of Morgan Stanley's workplace channel, which provides clients' employees with benefits like equity compensation, retirement plans and other executive services.
Morgan Stanley and Bank of America Corp. wrapped up third-quarter earnings announcements for the biggest US banks Wednesday in a quarter marked a stark divergence between the performance of equities and fixed-income trading desks. Bond traders are grappling with rising interest rates, which can crimp client activity, while stock traders have notched record after record this year on volatility fueled demand.
In the years following the 2008 financial crisis, Morgan Stanley executives reshaped the firm to focus more on wealth management and less on trading and investment banking. It has swelled into a $8.4 trillion juggernaut in the space, boosted by acquisitions along the way.
Total revenue from the trading operation was $7.81 billion, compared with expectations for $7.31 billion, according to a Wednesday. Wealth management revenue jumped to $9.1 billion from $8.2 billion a year earlier. Net income was $4.97 billion, up from $4.66 billion a year earlier.
Shares of Morgan Stanley, up 5.1% through Tuesday, advanced 0.5% in early New York trading.
Unlike most of its peers, Morgan Stanley's equities business has long been the larger of the two. The firm used to be the biggest stock-trading shop on Wall Street, but Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has claimed that title in recent years.
Morgan Stanley's investment bankers, meanwhile, posted $2.16 billion in net revenue, compared with $2.11 billion a year earlier.

item.title: Hotter-than-expected inflation report puts prospect of October rate hike back in play
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Hotter-than-expected inflation report puts prospect of October rate hike back in play
2026-10-14
Por Jennifer Schonberger

item.title: ASML Raises Full-Year Sales Outlook as AI Boom Drives Demand
item.author: Sarah Jacob
item.description:
ASML Raises Full-Year Sales Outlook as AI Boom Drives Demand
2026-10-14
Por Sarah Jacob
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/asml-raises-full-sales-outlook-051236633.html
(Bloomberg) -- ASML Holding NV upgraded the low end of its 2026 sales forecast, the third consecutive quarter it raised its outlook, as soaring artificial intelligence spending boosts demand for the Dutch company's chip-making machines.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The Veldhoven, Netherlands-based firm projected annual sales of between €44 billion ($49 billion) and €45 billion this year, it said in a statement Wednesday. The low end of the range was previously €43 billion.
ASML is the only company that makes the cutting-edge lithography machines used to produce semiconductors for the data centers powering the AI boom. Its outlook offers an indication of investment plans by chipmakers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Samsung Electronics Co. and Intel Corp. as spending on AI infrastructure surges.
Industry players are increasingly questioning whether the AI boom is sustainable. There was a global selloff in semiconductor stocks this week after Broadcom Inc. Chief Executive Officer Hock Tan likened investor sentiment in the industry to a casino.
ASML's results can provide a window into chipmakers' plans because the company's advanced tools have a lead time of more than a year between order and delivery.
Net sales in the July to September quarter rose to €11.66 billion, ASML said. That compares with the average analyst estimate of €11.7 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
Investors are also looking for indications that ASML can fulfill orders while the market is hot. In July, ASML said it plans to boost capacity by 30% next year for its second-most advanced tool, the low NA extreme ultraviolet lithography machine, which would take its annual shipment target to about 85 units.
ASML said it would not fully meet demand in 2027 and 2028.
Some customers "are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030," Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said in the statement. "We are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase we previously communicated."
The company is working to ship tools faster to customers by reducing the cycle time, or the period between starting production in its clean rooms and shipping a completed machine. It began construction on its second industrial campus in the Netherlands, the first phase of which is set to be completed in 2029.

item.title: Netflix Cuts 1,000 Jobs After Earlier Layoff Warnings
item.author: Desconocido
item.description:
Netflix Cuts 1,000 Jobs After Earlier Layoff Warnings
2026-10-14
Por Desconocido
https://www.forbes.com/sites/rickellis/2026/10/14/netflix-cuts-1000-jobs-after-earlier-layoff-warnings/
An aerial view of the Netflix logo displayed at Netflix studios, with the Hollywood sign in the distance. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)
Getty Images
Netflix is eliminating roughly 1,000 jobs worldwide, or about 6% of its workforce, in its largest round of layoffs since 2022,
The Wall Street Journal
reported Wednesday.
The cuts come as the streaming giant contends with slowing growth and concerns about subscriber engagement, while reassessing which areas of its expanding business are delivering results.
According to the Journal, Netflix co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos informed employees of the reductions in an email Wednesday morning. The bulk of the cuts will affect the company’s product, technology, legal and human resources teams, according to the report.
The Journal’s report follows earlier coverage from my Too Much TV Newsletter,
which first reported on Oct. 1
that Netflix was preparing for a major round of layoffs that could affect as many as 1,000 employees, or approximately 5% of its workforce. I reported that the cuts reflected both slowing engagement and pressure on the company’s stock, as well as an effort to shift resources away from underperforming divisions and areas executives viewed as having limited revenue potential.
Netflix’s push into physical experiences has been one area of particular scrutiny. Greg Lombardo, who led the company’s retail efforts, including its Netflix House attractions in Philadelphia and Dallas, is leaving after seven years. His departure followed the earlier exit of Pam Levine, the company’s former vice president of marketing and publicity for the U.S. and Canada.
I reported that sources inside Netflix viewed the retail and experiential business as promising but said the company had not yet figured out how to make the initiatives justify their costs through engagement and other returns.
Gaming also remains an open question. Netflix has spent heavily on its games business but has struggled to establish a meaningful position in the competitive market. The company closed its Hollywood-based Night School Studio in August and also announced plans to close its Helsinki-based Moonloot studio. Ellis reported that further changes in the division were possible.
The restructuring comes as Netflix faces increased
scrutiny over engagement and competition for viewers’ time
In a recent interview at Bloomberg’s Screentime conference,
Sarandos acknowledged that Netflix was not growing as quickly as he wanted
. The company has continued to pursue new programming and distribution opportunities even as it looks to sharpen spending and prioritize initiatives that can generate stronger returns.
The layoffs also recall Netflix’s 2022 restructuring, when the company cut hundreds of jobs amid a difficult period for the streaming business.
I noted in my initial report
that some executives view those earlier cuts as a precedent for a broader strategic reset, rather than simply a cost-reduction exercise.
For Netflix, the latest reductions represent an effort to recalibrate the company after years of expansion into adjacent businesses. The precise impact across individual divisions remains to be fully established, but the combination of workforce reductions and leadership departures suggests that the company is taking a harder look at where it invests and how it measures success.

item.title: AI bubble worriers should put this risk on their radar
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
AI bubble worriers should put this risk on their radar
2026-10-14
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/ai-bubble-worriers-should-put-this-risk-on-their-radar-164646098.html
AI bubble worriers should be more concerned about supply risk as companies build out AI infrastructure than with valuations being above historical norms.
After all, if tech companies can't get the equipment they need — such as AI and memory chips — there is no way they can meet robust profit predictions. Then the bubble will probably get popped.
"I think the concern that probably should be top of mind is less about some major faltering and demand, but supply chain risks and access to what is needed to continue this build-out," Charles Schwab chief investment strategist Liz Ann Sonders said on Sozzi Unleashed. "I think that is something that is less discussed, not to mention the fact that AI, even if long term it's disinflationary, it is inflationary in the here and now."
The debate over an AI bubble remains top of mind for investors.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today, with Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Microsoft (MSFT) representing over 21% of the index, per data from Creative Planning.
The importance of these three stocks to the S&P 500 has never been greater.
Only IBM (IBM), AT&T (T), and ExxonMobil (XOM) could hold a candle to the three tech stalwarts of today: In the mid-1980s, those three industrial giants at their peak made up 13.4% of the S&P 500.
The most crowded trade in October is being long global semiconductor stocks, according to BofA's latest fund manager survey. An AI bubble bursting was the second-highest risk on fund managers' minds, behind only rising Treasury yields.
"I think that's another factor to consider as it relates to what could maybe slow things down from an AI perspective," Sonders added. "It's just the cost of this build-out has moved up so, so significantly."

AI bubble worriers should be more concerned about supply risk as companies build out AI infrastructure than with valuations being above historical norms.
After all, if tech companies can't get the equipment they need — such as AI and memory chips — there is no way they can meet robust profit predictions. Then the bubble will probably get popped.
"I think the concern that probably should be top of mind is less about some major faltering and demand, but supply chain risks and access to what is needed to continue this build-out," Charles Schwab chief investment strategist Liz Ann Sonders said on Sozzi Unleashed. "I think that is something that is less discussed, not to mention the fact that AI, even if long term it's disinflationary, it is inflationary in the here and now."
The debate over an AI bubble remains top of mind for investors.
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today, with Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Microsoft (MSFT) representing over 21% of the index, per data from Creative Planning.
The importance of these three stocks to the S&P 500 has never been greater.
Only IBM (IBM), AT&T (T), and ExxonMobil (XOM) could hold a candle to the three tech stalwarts of today: In the mid-1980s, those three industrial giants at their peak made up 13.4% of the S&P 500.
The most crowded trade in October is being long global semiconductor stocks, according to BofA's latest fund manager survey. An AI bubble bursting was the second-highest risk on fund managers' minds, behind only rising Treasury yields.
"I think that's another factor to consider as it relates to what could maybe slow things down from an AI perspective," Sonders added. "It's just the cost of this build-out has moved up so, so significantly."

item.title: Fed’s Hammack warns inflation is persistent, demands more restrictive policy
item.author: Jennifer Schonberger
item.description:
Fed’s Hammack warns inflation is persistent, demands more restrictive policy
2026-10-14
Por Jennifer Schonberger
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/feds-hammack-warns-inflation-is-persistent-favors-more-restrictive-policy-185835420.html
Cleveland Federal Reserve president Beth Hammack said Monday that inflation is broad-based and will take time to come back down, even with a boost in interest rates.
Hammack said she is looking toward more frequent, smaller rate adjustments to ensure an inflationary mindset doesn't take hold.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
"I see inflation pressures as relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component," Hammack said, pointing to rising energy prices, tariffs, and AI. "And it's not just the supply side. Demand-side pressures coming from the AI build-out are raising prices."
Hammack noted that while a one-time increase in tariffs could potentially be viewed as a one-time increase in price levels, multiple waves of tariff increases have resulted in a series of cost shocks.
She also noted how the AI build-out is raising prices on key computer, electronic, and high-tech components, which is raising costs for data centers, but also for projects that use similar components in aviation, electricity production, and construction.
She says when she talks with contacts across her district, she hears about additional cost pressures in health insurance, plastics, metals, grains, electricity, and other areas. Hammack noted price pressures are also showing up in core services inflation excluding housing, a category that shouldn't be especially exposed to tariffs or energy.
"Because of the breadth of inflationary pressures, my baseline forecast is that it will take some time for inflation to return to 2%, even with appropriate monetary policy," said Hammack.
While a decline in energy prices would help move inflation in the right direction, she said the demand-side pressures are not "self-correcting."
"They are likely to be more persistent and usually require a more restrictive policy to rein them in," said Hammack.
Headline inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the Personal Consumption Expenditures index — was 3.4% in August. Adjusting for volatile food and energy prices, it was 3%. Both are above year-earlier levels, when headline was 2.7% and core was 2.9%. Officials will get a fresh reading on inflation this week when the Consumer Price Index — a different inflation measure — is released.
Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation
Hammack warned that with each month inflation remains high, it raises the risk of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy. She said she's beginning to see signs from business contacts that may be taking hold.

item.title: Why JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon is concerned about large global fiscal deficits
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Why JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon is concerned about large global fiscal deficits
2026-10-14
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/why-jpmorgan-ceo-jamie-dimon-is-concerned-about-large-global-fiscal-deficits-230317415.html
JPMorgan Chase (JPM) CEO Jamie Dimon still sees ballooning US deficits as a major hazard.
It's one of the key risks called out in the bank's earnings release on Tuesday, alongside "sticky inflation" and "elevated asset prices."
Dimon told Yahoo Finance on a media call that he "wouldn't use the word most concerned" when describing his views on large deficits relative to the other economic risks he mentioned.
However, Dimon continued, "I think it's a global issue about these global deficits. They haven't been going down, and you know, it includes China and includes Europe and includes other countries and stuff like that. And I don't know when and how that might bite. I just think it creates another source of, you know, potential risk. So then change, you know, it also changes the supply and demand of capital, which you see both there and [with] AI."
Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally
JPMorgan reported mixed second quarter earnings. The bottom line fell short of estimates, but it gave a more upbeat outlook for 2027 than some expected.
Shares pared losses in response.

item.title: Trump’s spree of new project announcements in recent weeks mirrors the run-up to the 2018 midterms
item.author: Ben Werschkul
item.description:
Trump’s spree of new project announcements in recent weeks mirrors the run-up to the 2018 midterms
2026-10-14
Por Ben Werschkul
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/trumps-spree-of-new-project-announcements-mirrors-the-run-up-to-the-2018-midterms-204037480.html
President Trump has been appearing around the US in the run-up to the midterm elections, announcing economic development projects — from a possible pipeline in Alaska to a steel plant in Iowa to an aluminum smelter in Oklahoma — that he says will transform the country.
"In the real economy, we are blowing it away," he said at a weekend stop in Tennessee.
Trump's message of confidence comes as the ultimate shape of these projects remains far from certain and often directly echoes his pitch at this stage in the 2018 midterm elections, a Yahoo Finance review found.
That election eight years ago was the last time Trump faced midterm voters and also saw him tout projects — most notably a Foxconn electronics manufacturing plant planned for Wisconsin — that turned out to be less than advertised.
"FoxConn … had a ribbon-cutting a few months ago," Trump said at a stop in Wisconsin on the eve of the 2018 election, pledging that the project was set to bring in "almost 15,000 jobs and there is no plant like it in the United States."
But the company eventually scrapped much of its manufacturing plans at the site and shifted the focus to data centers. Today, it employs only a reported 1,200 people at the site.
The president's penchant for promises is on display again as Election Day nears.
On Tuesday, he is set to travel to Alaska to tout a proposed $50 billion gas pipeline between South Korea and Alaska that could help Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan fend off a Democratic challenge.
Trump unveiled the project earlier this month in the Oval Office with Sullivan at his side, but South Korean officials immediately pushed back, saying no final investment decision has been made.
Korean President Lee Jae Myung even added that the deal will only proceed once the project's "commercial viability is confirmed."
Trump's promises in recent weeks have also included a $4 billion aluminum processing plant in Oklahoma. But local opposition to that plan — citing possible toxic chemicals and rising electricity prices — has led the town's mayor and a board of trustees to pause zoning approvals, leaving the fate of the project up in the air.
Even the project's developers recently reported to the SEC that "to complete this project, we will need to obtain substantial additional financing, and there can be no assurance that such financing will be available."
That didn't slow Trump from saying earlier this month that it would be "the largest aluminum factory, perhaps in the world, and you're going to make a fortune with it, lots of jobs, a lot of everything."

item.title: Why BlackRock is suddenly more bearish on stocks
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Why BlackRock is suddenly more bearish on stocks
2026-10-14
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/why-blackrock-is-suddenly-more-bearish-on-stocks-172414647.html
When BlackRock (BLK) gets more bearish on stocks, it's a red flag to toss onto the investing field.
The world's largest asset manager on Tuesday upgraded its views on US Treasurys, preferring short-term bonds as higher yields improve potential. The research was conducted by BlackRock's Jean Boivin, Rick Rieder, and Wei Li.
In turn, the team downgraded its views on US stocks to Neutral.
"Higher yields and potentially excessive Fed tightening expectations create room to unwind our U.S. Treasury underweight — a mainstay for most of the last six years," BlackRock's team said. "We upgrade Treasuries, favoring short-term bonds. In turn, we take profits: downgrading U.S. equities to neutral to manage potential volatility around the AI buildout."
They remain optimistic on AI stocks, however, despite the fresh concerns.
"We retain our conviction in AI fundamentals and preference for AI within U.S. equities," the strategists added.
BlackRock's downgrade in stocks comes at a precarious time for the market's non-AI areas. Sell-offs have gained steam amid the push higher in US Treasury yields, which has raised the cost of capital for companies that may not be growing as fast as AI companies.
About 84% of S&P 500 (^GSPC) stocks are now trading at least 10% below their all-time highs, according to new analysis from the Kobeissi Letter.
What's more, 59% of S&P 500 stocks are down at least 20% from their highs, 41% are down more than 30%, and 17% are off by more than 50%.
"I would say [it's] not a crisis but an eye-opener, and it's something I think you've got to think about," Rieder said about the move in yields on Sozzi Unleashed in late September.
